Article Title: In 2012, conservationists began working to remove an obsolete Massachusetts dam; 14 years later, demolition started to reconnect 7 miles of stream and restore 6 acres of wetland
Article Text:
Duxbury, MassachusettsRepresentative image

A dam with no purpose

A long road to removal

What the removal will achieve

A collaborative effort

A model for river restoration

A river reborn

For more than a century, a small concrete dam stood in the way of a river’s natural flow. Built to serve industries that no longer exist, the Temple Street Dam in Duxbury, Massachusetts, had long outlived its purpose. It blocked fish from reaching their spawning grounds, trapped sediment, created a maintenance burden for the town and disrupted the natural hydrology of the South River. In 2012, conservationists began working to change that. Fourteen years later, in 2026, demolition finally started. The removal of the Temple Street Dam is set to reconnect more than 7 miles of stream, restore 6 acres of open water wetland and bring the South River one step closer to the free-flowing ecosystem it once was, as shared by Town of Duxbury Massachusetts' website.The Temple Street Dam, also known as the Boys & Girls Club Dam #2, is located on the South River in Plymouth County, Massachusetts. Like many small dams across the state, it was built to support local industry; in this case, a mill that operated in the 19th and early 20th centuries. But those industries are long gone, and the dam now serves no functional purpose.Instead, it creates problems. The structure blocks all fish migration upstream, preventing species such as river herring, American eel and wild brook trout from reaching critical habitat.It traps sediment, which can degrade water quality and alter the river’s natural flow. And it requires ongoing maintenance from the Town of Duxbury, which owns the dam and is responsible for its upkeep.For years, the dam was simply accepted as part of the landscape. But as awareness of the ecological impacts of obsolete dams grew, so did the movement to remove them.The push to remove the Temple Street Dam began in earnest in 2012, when the North and South Rivers Watershed Association (NSRWA) and local partners started exploring the possibility. The South River originates in the red maple swamps of Duxbury and flows to Massachusetts Bay in Marshfield. It is a vital waterway for migratory fish, wildlife and the surrounding communities.In 2016, the Massachusetts Division of Ecological Restoration (DER) identified the South River Restoration Project as a priority. The project includes the potential removal of three dams along the river: Temple Street, Chandler Pond and Veterans Memorial Park. The goal is to restore fish passage, improve habitat and reduce the maintenance burden on the towns of Duxbury and Marshfield.The first dam to come down was the Veterans Memorial Park Dam, removed in January 2025. The Temple Street Dam is the final barrier on the South River, and its removal marks the culmination of more than a decade of planning, permitting and community engagement.The removal of the Temple Street Dam is expected to deliver significant ecological benefits. By eliminating the barrier, the project will:Reconnect an additional 7 miles of stream, allowing fish and other aquatic species to move freely upstream and downstreamRestore 6 acres of open water wetland, creating habitat for wildlife and improving water qualityRestore natural hydrology, reducing the risk of flooding and improving the river’s resilience to climate changeEliminate the ongoing maintenance burden on the Town of DuxburyThe project also includes the construction of a three-step riffle/pool stream segment to replace the dam. This will ensure passage for fish and other aquatic species, restore ecological processes and maintain natural hydrology while avoiding downstream flood impacts to infrastructure.The Temple Street Dam Removal Project is the result of collaboration between multiple partners, including the Town of Duxbury, the North and South Rivers Watershed Association, the Massachusetts Division of Ecological Restoration and MassBays. Funding has come from state grants, including a $150,000 award from the Healey-Driscoll Administration in 2026 to support construction.Public engagement has also been a key component. In October 2023, NSRWA and project partners held public information sessions to present the current design for the removal and gather feedback from the community. The project team has worked closely with local residents, conservation groups and government agencies to ensure the removal is done safely and effectively.The removal of the Temple Street Dam is part of a broader movement to restore rivers and wetlands across Massachusetts. Over the past two decades, more than 100 dams have been removed in the state, reconnecting thousands of miles of stream and restoring critical habitat for fish and wildlife.These projects are not just about removing barriers. They are about reconnecting landscapes, restoring natural processes and building resilience to climate change. Healthy rivers and wetlands provide a range of ecological services, including floodwater storage, water filtration and habitat for biodiversity.The South River Restoration Project is a prime example of what can be achieved when communities, conservationists and government agencies work together. It is a model for how obsolete infrastructure can be replaced with living, breathing ecosystems that benefit both people and nature.As demolition of the Temple Street Dam begins, the South River is on the cusp of a transformation. For the first time in more than a century, fish will be able to swim freely up and down the river. Wetlands will be restored, water quality will improve and the natural flow of the river will be re-established.The project is a reminder that even small actions, like removing a single dam, can have big impacts. It is a testament to the power of persistence, collaboration and a shared vision for a healthier, more resilient future.In 2012, conservationists began working to remove an obsolete dam. Fourteen years later, that work is finally bearing fruit. And when the last piece of concrete is removed, the South River will flow freely once again, a living symbol of what is possible when we choose to restore rather than restrict, to reconnect rather than divide.
Article Summary: The Temple Street Dam in Duxbury, Massachusetts, will be removed in 2026. The dam was built in the 19th and early 20th centuries to support local industry. It blocked fish from reaching their spawning grounds, trapped sediment and disrupted the natural hydrology of the South River.

Article Title: Six generations have vacationed at New Hampshire's Lake Winnipesaukee; one family still spends thousands each summer to keep the tradition alive
Article Text:
Representative image

A tradition that began generations ago

Why they keep returning, even when it’s expensive

The pull of a familiar place

Memories of the making across generations

The difficulty of keeping up traditions

Why the lake still matters

For one family, summer has always meant Lake Winnipesaukee in New Hampshire. Over six generations, the lake has been the backdrop for childhood swims, boat rides, family meals and countless reunions. Today, even though many members live only an hour away, they still spend thousands of dollars each summer to keep the tradition alive.The decision is not purely financial. It is rooted in nostalgia, identity and the desire to preserve a shared sense of belonging. For this family, the lake is not just a destination. It is a place where their history has been written, one summer at a time.Kelly Burch wrote about her family's story on Business Insider. Here's what she shared:The family’s connection to Lake Winnipesaukee stretches back more than a century. Their ancestors first started vacationing in the same cove, renting or staying in nearby homes as the lake became a popular summer retreat in New England.Over time, as children grew up and had their own families, the tradition expanded. Cousins, aunts, uncles and grandparents all returned to the same area each year. Some branches of the family eventually bought their own properties around the lake, while others continued renting in the same neighbourhood, Burch shared.The result is a multigenerational network that still gathers in the same cove their ancestors once visited. Even when the exact house changes, the location remains meaningful. The lake itself becomes a constant in a world where so much else shifts.But maintaining a summer tradition at a popular lake is not cheap, Burch said. Rental prices around Lake Winnipesaukee can run into the thousands of dollars per week, especially during peak season. Add in boat rentals, groceries, activities and meals out, and the total cost of a summer trip can be substantial.Yet for this family, the expense is justified by the value of the experience. They have tried vacationing in new places, but nothing has matched the emotional resonance of returning to the lake. The familiarity of the water, the shoreline and the surrounding towns creates a sense of continuity that is difficult to replicate elsewhere.Nostalgia plays a powerful role. Adults who spent their own childhood summers at Winnipesaukee want their children and grandchildren to have similar memories. They want the next generation to know the same coves, beaches and boat routes that shaped their own summers.In that sense, the money spent is not just on accommodation and activities. It is an investment in family identity and shared history, she said.Lake Winnipesaukee is New Hampshire’s largest lake, with more than 70 miles of shoreline, numerous islands and a long history as a summer destination. Towns around the lake, such as Wolfeboro, Meredith and Laconia, have catered to vacationers for generations.For families with deep roots in the area, the lake offers more than scenery. It gives structure to rituals: morning swims, evening boat rides, favourite ice cream spots, yearly meetings and known paths around the water.These small traditions accumulate over time. A particular bench where the family eats pizza, a specific spot where they watch fireworks, a routine morning paddle before the rest of the group wakes up, all of these become part of the family story.Returning to the same place makes it easier to maintain those rituals. There is no need to relearn the area or discover new favourite spots. Instead, each summer builds on the last.For the kids, the lake is where cousins become best friends, where summer is measured in water play and shared experiences. For adults, it’s an opportunity to meet with brothers and sisters, parents and extended family in a relaxed setting.Older generations may remember the lake from decades ago, while younger members experience the lake through modern-day activities such as paddleboarding, kayaking and waterskiing. But the central experience is still the same: time together outside the daily routine.Many families at Winnipesaukee create their own version of this pattern. Some stay at long-standing resorts where multiple generations have returned for decades. Others rent homes in the same neighbourhoods year after year. A few own cottages that have been passed down through the family.What unites them is the desire to keep a shared summer tradition alive, even as life becomes busier and more dispersed.It is not always easy to keep a multigenerational tradition alive. Schedules become more complex as families grow. Work, school schedules, sports and other activities can make it tough to coordinate a large group.Another consideration is cost. Lake Winnipesaukee is a popular destination with high demand for lake rentals boats and dining driving up prices. For some families, the only way to ensure a return every year is to buy property. For some people, renting is still the most flexible, even if it is expensive.And then there’s the question whether the younger generations want to keep the tradition going. Some might prefer other kinds of holidays, or be less attached to the lake than their parents and grandparents.Families that succeed often adapt. They may shorten the length of the trip, adjust the timing, or allow different branches of the family to visit at slightly different times while still maintaining the core connection to the lake.For the family that has spent six summers at Winnipesaukee across generations, the lake represents more than a vacation spot. It is a place where their story took place. This is where grandparents once rocked babies who are now grown, where cousins learned to swim together and where family milestones have been marked.That history is honoured is a way of returning each summer. It is also a way to make sure that the next generation has a place of its own in the family story.In a world of endless travel choices and new destinations appearing all the time, it might seem strange to pick the same lake year after year. But familiarity is the thing with this family. This lake is more than a place they go to. It’s part of who they are.
Article Summary: The Burch family has been visiting Lake Winnipesaukee in New Hampshire for six generations. The family spends thousands of dollars each summer to keep the tradition alive. The decision is rooted in nostalgia, identity and the desire to preserve a shared sense of belonging.

Article Title: Candace Owens says she feels Charlie Kirk is “fighting alongside” her as she opens up about his assassination
Article Text:
Candace Owens reflects on Charlie Kirk’s assassination

Candace Owens links grief, conviction and her audience

Candace Owens has offered a deeply personal account of how her feelings surrounding Charlie Kirk ’s assassination have changed, saying she no longer feels consumed by the initial trauma. In a video shared on social media, Owens described feeling that Kirk is spiritually “with us” as she continues her work. Her remarks quickly drew attention because of the striking image accompanying the discussion and the way she connected grief, faith and her public mission.Speaking from behind a microphone, Owens explained that her reaction to Kirk’s death has shifted over time. Rather than describing herself as haunted by the initial shock, she said she now feels a sense of spiritual connection to the late conservative activist.Owens framed that feeling as part of a broader belief that people are becoming more spiritually aware. She also connected her optimism to her conviction that truth ultimately prevails."And I do think that spiritually, like people are, we're just kind of more in tune right now. And like I said, the reason why I'm positive every day and happy every day is because the truth is inevitable. It always wins.And I know that I am on the side of truth. And like I said, I do also just, I'm in a different place right now with the assassination of the Charlie being gone, where I have moved from that initial trauma and feeling haunted by it to feeling like he's just like fighting alongside.And I don't know if that makes sense to you guys, but I, that's just how I feel, man.Call it added to my a pile of dreams or something. I feel like Charlie's really with us and we're going to see this thing to the end. Like he tweeted back in 2018, I won't be here, but you see this thing to the end.That's what we're doing. We're seeing it to the end. Uh, I want to remind you guys, if you would like to support the show, you can get merch available at Candice Owens.com."The comments are notable because Owens did not present her description of Kirk being “with us” as a literal claim that can be independently established. Instead, she described it as a personal spiritual feeling following a traumatic event.That distinction is important when discussing claims involving grief, faith and the afterlife. Her comments reflect her own interpretation rather than something that can be verified as fact.The setting of the video also became part of the discussion. Owens appeared seated at her podcast setup, speaking directly into the microphone while addressing viewers. The presentation gave the remarks a more intimate tone than a conventional political statement.Her language also showed how closely she connects personal belief with her broader public message. Owens said she believes she is on the “side of truth” and portrayed her continued work as part of a larger effort she intends to pursue.The final part of her remarks shifted toward support for her programme, with Owens encouraging viewers to purchase merchandise from her website. That transition has attracted attention because it followed an emotional discussion about Kirk, grief and spirituality.For audiences, the moment illustrates how political media can blend personal experiences, belief and audience engagement in the same conversation.Owens' remarks are likely to continue generating debate, particularly among viewers who interpret spiritual language differently. Some may see her words as an expression of grief and faith, while others may question the way such language is used within political media.What remains clear is that Owens says her own emotional response has changed. She described moving from feeling haunted by Kirk’s death to feeling motivated by what she believes his legacy represents.For Owens, that shift appears to have become part of how she understands the next chapter of her public work.
Article Summary: Candace Owens says she no longer feels haunted by the death of Charlie Kirk. In a video shared on social media, she describes feeling that Kirk is spiritually ‘with us’ Her remarks quickly drew attention because of the striking image accompanying the discussion.

Article Title: Twitch faces ‘furious’ streamer backlash as Amazon AI training opt-out appears enabled by default
Article Text:
Twitch faces ‘furious’ streamer backlash as Amazon AI training opt-out appears enabled by default

Why are Twitch streamers angry about the new Amazon AI training setting?

What did Twitch say about training streamer content for generative AI?

Twitch is facing criticism after a new setting appeared to allow Amazon to use streamer channel content to train generative AI models. The setting is turned on by default, meaning streamers have to change their privacy settings if they do not want their content used for this type of training. The issue came to light on August 12, 2026, when livestreaming reporter Zach Bussey shared details of the new option. Twitch later responded, saying the platform itself is not training GenAI models on streamer content, while confirming that the setting relates to Amazon’s generative AI training.Zach Bussey said streamers can “opt out of some training” through the “security and privacy” settings on their channels. The new option is called “training for generative AI” and includes this description:“Allow your channel content to train generative AI content models at Amazon. Turning this off does not opt you out of Twitch and Amaz0on using your channel content for other purposes described in the Twitch Privacy Notice, including using AI-supported Twitch features that benefit the community by facilitating streamer growth and monetization (such as real-time sponsorship campaign assistance), viewer discovery (such as recommendations), and community safety (such as AutoMod). ”The wording drew criticism because the setting was enabled by default.Users questioned why creators were not asked to actively agree before their content could be used for AI training. The reaction included strong comments on X.“Twitch keeps giving me reasons to hate it oh my gosh i feel vindicated” X user @NotFromStlouis commented.“You have to be a real scumbag to do this @Twitch. You KNOW if you asked for permission EVERYONE would say no. So you did what you knew would be denied if you asked permssion and you made it opt-out; just like every scumbag lacking scruples.” X user @HexerStoner remarked.“Why would they make it on by default?” X user @Soldi3rOfD wrote.“I will never understand the need of every billion dollar corporation that owns a social/entertainment platform to integrate AI or AI training into there applications. Like seriously who does this benefit in any meaningful capacity outside of advertisers…oh wait there it is.” X user @L4teSubmission stated.Twitch responded to the criticism on August 12, saying, “Just want to be clear. This lets you opt out of Amazon’s Generative AI content model training. Twitch is not training GenAI models on streamer content.”The response, however, received an X Community Note pointing out the relationship between the two companies: “Twitch Interactive Inc. and its affiliates are subsidiaries of Amazon.com, Inc. (“Amazon”).”The distinction is important. Twitch says it is not itself training the models, while the setting allows Amazon to use eligible Twitch channel content for generative AI training unless a streamer opts out. The option is available under Twitch’s Security and Privacy settings.
Article Summary: Twitch is facing criticism after a new setting appeared to allow Amazon to use streamer channel content to train generative AI models. The setting is turned on by default, meaning streamers have to change their privacy settings if they do not want their content used for this type of training. Twitch responded, saying the platform itself is not training GenAI models on streamer content.

Article Title: Clavicular’s old graduation video sparks massive reaction as fans discover the streamer’s life before fame
Article Text:
Clavicular’s middle school graduation video goes viral

Clavicular’s rise from looksmaxxing content to IRL streaming

A resurfaced video from the COVID-19 pandemic is giving fans a very different look at Clavicular before he became a major name in livestreaming. The footage shows the creator during his online middle school graduation, with his parents celebrating from home. The wholesome moment has quickly attracted attention because it offers a glimpse of the young student behind the controversial internet personality now known for IRL streams and looksmaxxing content.The resurfaced footage shows Clavicular, whose real name is Braden Peters, taking part in a virtual graduation ceremony during the pandemic. His name is announced before he receives his middle school certificate, while his parents can be seen celebrating the achievement from home.The simplicity of the clip has made it stand out against the image many viewers now associate with the streamer.Clavicular has built his online career around provocative content, livestreams and discussions about physical appearance. Seeing him in an ordinary school setting has therefore surprised some fans who only know him from his more recent internet presence.The video also puts his rapid rise into perspective. Just a few years ago, he was a student completing school remotely during one of the most unusual periods in recent history.Today, he has become a recognisable figure in the streaming world.According to the report, Clavicular is 20 years old and has developed a sizeable following across platforms. His audience has grown through a mixture of IRL broadcasts, self-improvement discussions and content connected to the online looksmaxxing community.His transformation from a middle school student appearing at a virtual ceremony to a widely discussed streamer has naturally made the old footage more fascinating to viewers.Clavicular initially gained attention by discussing physical appearance and ways people could improve their perceived attractiveness. His content later expanded into the broader online culture surrounding “looksmaxxing” and “mogging”.Those terms have become increasingly familiar across social media, particularly among younger internet audiences. Clavicular has used that interest to build a distinctive online identity, although his controversial approach has also brought criticism.His growing popularity has not been without setbacks. Several incidents involving the streamer have generated debate online, adding another layer to his increasingly polarising public image.More recently, Clavicular said he wanted to move away from his previous focus and explore what he called “geomaxing”. He described a plan to “move to countries with weaker economies” so he could “mog” people there.The comments sparked another wave of discussion. While geomaxing can broadly refer to moving to another country for factors such as lower living costs, lifestyle or better opportunities, Clavicular presented the idea through the lens of his existing appearance-focused content.That contrast helps explain why the graduation video has resonated with viewers. It shows a much quieter chapter of his life before controversy, viral clips and millions of social media views became part of his identity.The resurfaced footage does not reveal anything dramatic about Clavicular. Instead, its appeal comes from how ordinary it feels.His parents celebrating his graduation, a virtual ceremony and a young student receiving his certificate are far removed from the personality audiences see today.For fans who discovered Clavicular only after his streaming career took off, the clip offers a reminder that internet personalities can have surprisingly recent lives before fame changes everything.
Article Summary: Clavicular has built his online career around provocative content, livestreams and discussions about physical appearance. The resurfaced footage shows Clavicular taking part in a virtual graduation ceremony during the COVID-19 pandemic. His parents can be seen celebrating the achievement from home.

Article Title: Who was Jiang Xiaorou? The haunting story of the Chinese TikToker whose death brought her most controversial video back
Article Text:
Who was Jiang Xiaorou and why was she famous?

no evidence that the destruction of the statue caused the accident or that her death had any supernatural explanation

How did Jiang Xiaorou die?

Why did Jiang Xiaorou's Guanyin statue video become controversial?

Jiang Xiaorou's final legacy

Jiang Xiaorou, a 24-year-old Chinese paranormal content creator, has died following severe injuries sustained in a traffic accident in July. Known online for confronting supernatural beliefs and challenging traditional superstitions, she had built a large following on Douyin. Her death has now brought renewed attention to the provocative videos that made her famous, while her family has urged people to avoid speculation.Jiang Xiaorou, whose online persona was known as “Jiang Xiaorou Ya”, became recognised for content that deliberately pushed the boundaries of paranormal exploration. Her videos focused on abandoned places, supernatural claims and traditional taboos.Rather than simply discussing whether supernatural beliefs were real, she often presented herself as the person willing to test them. That approach helped her attract a substantial audience on Douyin, China's major short-video platform.Her content also made her controversial. One of the most widely discussed episodes came in 2025, when she filmed herself smashing a Guanyin statue with a hammer as part of an anti-superstition challenge. Reports say she was attempting to challenge the idea that disrespecting religious objects would lead to supernatural consequences.The video later became a major part of the discussion surrounding her death. However, there isJiang was reportedly involved in a serious traffic accident on July 15, 2026, while travelling between Guangxi and Guangzhou. She suffered critical injuries and was taken to hospital, where she remained in intensive care.Reports described severe brain injuries and damage to multiple organs. She reportedly spent weeks receiving treatment before dying on August 10, aged 24. Her death was subsequently confirmed through her social-media account and reports from people connected to her hometown.The tragedy has also drawn attention to her final piece of content before the crash. Her last reported video, posted on July 9, involved calls to mysterious telephone numbers suggested by followers. The eerie nature of the footage has encouraged some online users to search for connections between the video and the accident.Those connections remain unverified.Her family has specifically asked people to stop spreading speculation about her death and private life. They urged followers to respect the facts and remember Jiang with dignity.The Guanyin incident remains one of the defining moments of Jiang's online career. In the video, she destroyed a statue while challenging superstition. The stunt divided viewers, with some seeing it as an attempt to question deeply held beliefs and others considering it disrespectful.Following her death, the old footage resurfaced. Some social-media users began describing the accident as a form of punishment or karma.That interpretation is not supported by evidence.The circumstances of Jiang's death are tragic, but connecting a fatal traffic accident to a previous internet stunt turns an unverified belief into an apparent fact. Her family's appeal for restraint is therefore particularly important as old videos continue circulating online.Jiang Xiaorou built her audience by asking uncomfortable questions and taking risks that many viewers would not attempt themselves. Her content placed her at the centre of debates about superstition, religion and internet culture.Now, her death has created an unusual reversal. The creator who spent much of her career challenging supernatural explanations has become the subject of supernatural theories herself.For her family and followers, however, the central fact remains far simpler. Jiang Xiaorou died after suffering catastrophic injuries in a traffic accident. The viral theories surrounding her older videos remain speculation, not established explanations.
Article Summary: Jiang Xiaorou, 24, died after suffering severe injuries in a traffic accident. She was known online for confronting supernatural beliefs and challenging traditional superstitions. Her death has brought renewed attention to the provocative videos that made her famous, while her family has urged people to avoid speculation.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Karl Popper: 'Those who promise us paradise on earth never produced anything but a hell' and the deadly psychological flaw behind every political utopia
Article Text:
Karl Popper was a 20th-century philosopher who championed open societies, critical thinking, and gradual reform over utopian political schemes

"Those who promise us paradise on earth never produced anything but a hell."

Writing in exile while Europe burned

The Open Society and Its Enemies.

The psychology of utopian tyranny

Messy improvements over total overhauls

In 1919, a seventeen-year-old student in Vienna joined a street demonstration organized by young communists. Police opened fire on the unarmed crowd, killing twelve people and wounding dozens more. The young student had encouraged his friends to march because he believed that short-term violence was a necessary step toward an inevitable social utopia. Standing in the blood-stained street that afternoon, he experienced a complete collapse of faith. He realized that an ideology promising absolute perfection had pushed aside his moral judgment and led directly to human sacrifice.That student was Karl Popper, and the lesson of that afternoon stayed with him for the rest of his life. Decades later, he summed up his warning in a single observation:The quote cuts through political salesmanship and points to a repeated tragedy in human history. When leaders claim they have the perfect plan for creating a flawless society, they often demand great power to put that plan into action. Because perfection is impossible in a complex world, reality eventually resists the plan. Instead of admitting that their theory has failed, utopian leaders blame human weakness.They label critics as enemies of paradise who must be silenced, re-educated, or eliminated.The promise of earthly perfection can become a moral blank cheque, allowing immediate cruelty to be justified in the name of future happiness.Karl Popper published this observation in his 1945 masterwork,Born in Vienna in 1902 to a Jewish family that had converted to Lutheranism, Popper left Austria in 1937 as fascism spread across Central Europe. He accepted a lectureship in philosophy at Canterbury University College in Christchurch, New Zealand, where he lived in relative isolation during the Second World War.Popper described The Open Society and Its Enemies as his personal contribution to the war effort. He wrote the two-volume work in his small office in Christchurch between 1938 and 1943. The book tried to identify the intellectual roots of totalitarianism while Allied forces were fighting Axis armies across Europe and Asia.In Chapter 18 of the second volume, Popper directly criticized utopian social engineering. He compared it with what he called "piecemeal social engineering."His main target was a philosophical tradition stretching from Plato through Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel to Karl Marx. Popper argued that these thinkers had fallen into what he called "historicism", the mistaken belief that history follows fixed laws toward a predetermined destination.When political leaders accept historicist thinking, they can begin to see human lives as expendable parts of some final social structure.Popper's criticism rests on a basic idea about knowledge: human beings are naturally fallible.In his philosophy of science, Popper argued that no amount of observation can prove a theory completely correct, but one clear counter-example can show that it is false. He believed political theories should be treated in a similar way and should remain open to testing and criticism.Utopian schemes break this rule because they treat their final goal as obvious and unquestionable. If a political blueprint cannot be challenged, it cannot be corrected when it fails.A piecemeal reformer introduces a small policy change, such as adjusting a tax rate or building a local clinic. The results can then be measured. If the policy fails, it can be changed or removed without destroying the whole society.A utopian planner works in the opposite way. Because the goal is total transformation, failure is often blamed on enemies, institutional resistance, or a lack of commitment.The French Revolution's Reign of Terror in 1793 offers a clear historical example. Maximilien Robespierre wanted to create a "Republic of Virtue" based on the political ideas of Jean-Jacques Rousseau. To create perfect virtue, Robespierre came to believe that terror was necessary. Thousands were sent to the guillotine to defend an ideal that existed mainly in his mind.Similar patterns appeared in the 20th century, from Stalin's forced collectivization during the Five-Year Plans to the Khmer Rouge's attempt to create an agrarian socialist state in Cambodia, where an estimated two million people died between 1975 and 1979.Popper's warning remains relevant to modern institutions, public policy, and technology.In corporate management and Silicon Valley companies, founders often use grand mission statements about changing society or creating friction-free economies. When platform algorithms designed to increase user engagement end up spreading political extremism or harming young people's mental health, executives may continue defending the larger vision instead of dealing with the immediate damage.The technology industry's desire for total disruption can resemble the utopian mindset Popper warned about: putting an imagined future ahead of people's needs and wellbeing today.In government, the quote offers a useful way to judge political promises. Candidates who promise complete overhauls of complicated systems, whether healthcare, energy, or international trade, can underestimate the unexpected effects of rapid, top-down change.Good leadership requires accepting that society is too complicated for one person or one authority to control through a grand design.In a 1989 interview published in Le Monde, Popper again argued that political action should focus on reducing real suffering rather than trying to create perfect happiness."Work for the elimination of concrete evils rather than for the realization of abstract goods," Popper insisted. "Do not aim at establishing happiness by political means. Rather aim at the elimination of concrete miseries."By rejecting promises of total perfection, open societies protect people's right to criticize their leaders, correct mistakes through peaceful elections, and make small, measurable improvements without destroying the whole system to fix a problem.
Article Summary: Karl Popper was a 20th-century philosopher who championed open societies, critical thinking, and gradual reform over utopian political schemes. Popper wrote The Open Society and Its Enemies as his personal contribution to the war effort. He compared utopian social engineering with "piecemeal social engineering"

Article Title: Why Putin’s first Kuril Islands visit matters as Russia-Japan ties hit new low
Article Text:

Putin visits Iturup, inspects local industry

Why the Kuril Islands are disputed

Japan protests Putin's visit

Ukraine war deepens Russia-Japan tensions

Visit comes amid wider military tensions in the region

Ukraine battlefield developments add to regional backdrop

No breakthrough in decades-old territorial dispute

Russian President Vladimir Putin has visited the disputed Kuril Islands for the first time, travelling to Iturup as Moscow's relations with Japan remain deeply strained over Russia's war in Ukraine.The visit, reported by Russian state media on Thursday, comes after Putin oversaw military exercises involving Russia's Pacific Fleet in the country's Far East.It also comes a day after North Korea, a close Russian ally, fired a ballistic missile towards waters off the Korean Peninsula.Putin's trip to Iturup is significant because the island is among four southern Kuril Islands that Japan claims as its own territory and calls the Northern Territories.According to Reuters, Putin visited the Yasny fish-processing plant on Iturup and was shown local fishing operations. Russian television footage showed him examining large tuna and halibut and sampling fish roe.The Russian president also interacted with residents."What lovely weather you have there, just like a resort!" Putin told a group of locals.The visit followed Putin's inspection of the Pacific Fleet's flagship missile cruiser Varyag during military exercises in Russia's Far East.Russian state news agency TASS described the Iturup trip as Putin's first personal visit to the Kuril island chain.Putin had previously visited Sakhalin but had not personally travelled to the disputed islands.The dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces seized the Kuril Islands after the Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945.The four islands at the centre of the dispute are Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets. Japan refers to them as Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai Islands and maintains that they are Japanese territory.The Soviet Union retained control of the islands after the war, and Russia has maintained a military presence there.The islands are strategically important because of their location between the Russian Far East and northern Japan. They also have rich fishing grounds and deposits of minerals, including gold and silver.Around 20,000 people currently live on the islands under Russian administration, while Japan says its former residents were displaced following the Soviet takeover. Around 17,000 Japanese residents were deported after the islands were occupied in 1945.Putin's visit has drawn a strong reaction from Tokyo.Japanese foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi protested the visit, reiterating Japan's claim over the islands."The northern territories, including Etorofu, are Japan's inherent territory both historically and based on international law," Motegi said, according to Reuters."Japan strongly protests this visit."The territorial dispute has prevented Russia and Japan from signing a formal peace treaty formally ending their World War II conflict.There have been several attempts to resolve the dispute over the decades. In 1956, Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev suggested that two of the disputed islands could be returned to Japan as part of a peace settlement, although no final agreement followed.Negotiations resumed after the collapse of the Soviet Union, but the territorial dispute remained unresolved.The long-running dispute has become more difficult to resolve since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.Japan joined Western countries in imposing sanctions on Moscow and has strongly supported Ukraine. In response, Russia suspended peace treaty negotiations with Japan and halted several forms of economic cooperation relating to the disputed islands.Moscow has also accused Tokyo of adopting an increasingly hostile position towards Russia.Putin used his address to Pacific Fleet personnel on Wednesday to criticise Japan's sanctions and its continuing territorial claims. He said Russia had previously maintained constructive relations with Tokyo over the issue during the administration of former Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, but claimed Japan had since changed its position.He noted that Japan's current territorial claims came despite what he described as the post-World War II territorial arrangements being reflected in international documents.Putin also recalled the 1956 Soviet-Japanese declaration, which restored diplomatic relations and opened the way towards a possible peace treaty and a settlement of the island dispute. He claimed that Tokyo later refused to abide by the declaration.Russia has increasingly strengthened its military presence and activities in its Far Eastern territories as tensions with Japan have risen.Putin's Kuril Islands trip also comes against a backdrop of increased military activity in the Asia-Pacific region.The Russian president had travelled to the Far East to oversee the final stage of large-scale Pacific Fleet exercises, which began on August 4.Putin said the exercises were necessary to maintain military readiness and protect Russia's interests and security in the Asia-Pacific region. He also accused NATO of seeking to increase its presence in the region.Putin warned of rising conflict potential in the Asia-Pacific and Arctic regions, while criticising what he described as plans to deploy new weapons systems in the region.The timing was notable because North Korea fired a ballistic missile on Wednesday, just days before major South Korea-US military exercises are scheduled to begin. Moscow and Pyongyang have significantly deepened their military partnership in recent years.Putin's visit comes as Russia's war in Ukraine continues with fighting and long-range strikes intensifying.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces had recaptured about 745 sq km of territory this year across parts of the southeastern front, including 26 settlements in the Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. However, these battlefield claims have not been independently verified.Ukraine has also stepped up attacks deep inside Russian territory, including a major recent strike on Novorossiysk, a key Black Sea port and grain-export hub.The attack reportedly damaged port infrastructure and disrupted operations at major grain terminals.Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter, making Novorossiysk strategically important not only for Moscow but also for global agricultural markets.At the same time, Russia has continued missile and drone strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.For Japan, Putin's visit is likely to further complicate already strained relations with Moscow.The Kuril Islands remain one of the most enduring territorial disputes left over from World War II.While there have been periods of diplomatic engagement and economic cooperation, neither side has been able to agree on a final settlement.With Russia's war in Ukraine having pushed Moscow and Tokyo further apart, Putin's first personal visit to the disputed islands sends a strong political signal that Russia has no immediate intention of softening its position over territory it has controlled since 1945.
Article Summary: Putin visited Iturup, one of the four southern Kuril Islands that Japan claims as its own territory. The dispute dates back to the final days of World War II, when Soviet forces seized the islands after the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. The islands are strategically important because of their location between the Russian Far East and Japan.

Article Title: Zelenskyy seeks 10% of US stockpile to 'destroy all Russians’ missiles’: Report
Article Text:
Zelensky urged the US to sell Ukraine 5-10% of its Patriot interceptor stockpile to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks

Zelensky describes daily efforts to secure missiles

Uncertainty over Ukraine's Patriot production

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you support the idea of the US providing more Patriot missiles to Ukraine? Yes, absolutely No, they should focus on diplomacy 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Zelensky seeks greater US role in peace talks

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged the United States to sell Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles, saying even 5% of the US stockpile would help Kyiv survive the winter, while 10% could allow it to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.Zelensky made the comments in an interview with CNN as Ukraine faces a sharp increase in Russian ballistic missile attacks and a severe shortage of Patriot interceptors.“This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025,” he said. “Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before.”“If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles. I have 1%.”Zelensky said Russia's intensified attacks had placed further pressure on Ukraine's air defences, particularly around Kyiv. The United Nations has said July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022.“Each night you have attacks, and four or five times per month we have massive attacks … terrible nights. Very heroic, very resilient people really. But they (are) tired.”Zelensky said securing additional interceptors had become a daily priority, involving direct appeals to the US and negotiations with other allies.“This is what I live each day: from 1% to 5%. I have some months, and million phone calls … I try to exchange something to missiles … I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s outside of the law. But I can’t speak about it.”He said the global supply of Patriot missiles had been strained by the US war with Iran, during which American and Gulf forces used dozens of interceptors against Iranian missile and drone attacks.The shortage has left Ukraine facing growing difficulty in defending its cities against Russian missile strikes.Zelensky also said uncertainty remained over a proposal for Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptor missiles under a US licence.US President Donald Trump had said during the Nato summit in Ankara that he would allow Ukraine to obtain a licence to manufacture the systems. However, Trump later expressed uncertainty about the proposal.Patriot system manufacturers have since sent officials to Kyiv to discuss potential production, but Zelensky said no agreement had yet been reached.“I hope that I will get it,” Zelensky said. “I don’t have now 5% and I don’t have such an acceptance. And this is for me is a big challenge, one of the biggest I had from the very beginning of this war.”Zelensky said he had been appealing directly to the White House through calls and messages, as well as through Ukraine's allies, to secure additional Patriot support.Zelensky also said Ukraine had presented new proposals for the US-led peace process, while calling for greater American involvement.“We need more involvement of the American side to the peace plan. I’m thankful to the team of President Trump that they want to continue. (Russian President Vladimir) Putin doesn’t want to stop this war now and (there’s) not enough pressure on him now.”He rejected the possibility of Ukraine surrendering the remaining territory in the Donbass sought by Russian President Vladimir Putin, saying security guarantees remained essential to prevent another invasion.“Russia begins to speak about this war, and they speak about territory. The key question is why he will not come again with 1 or 2 additional million soldiers after a big pause. Why he will not come again to occupy us?”Zelensky also backed Western assessments that Putin could eventually seek to escalate the conflict with Nato, including by targeting the Baltic states.“He doesn’t know how to end this war without big occupation or big victory for his society. It’s more simple to find some smaller country … for him, it will not be important if this country is in Nato or not in Nato. He wants quick victory, 100% sure that he will win, occupy or destroy or control.”
Article Summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has urged the United States to sell Ukraine more Patriot interceptor missiles. He said even 5% of the US stockpile would help Kyiv survive the winter, while 10% could allow it to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks. Zelenski said securing additional interceptors had become a daily priority.

Article Title: Indian-origin teen charged with murdering mother, brother in US after ‘kill family’ searches
Article Text:
Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts.

A 17-year-old Indian-origin teenager has been charged with allegedly murdering his mother and younger brother at their home in Acton, Massachusetts, authorities said.The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery on a household or family member and assault and battery, along with charges of using a vehicle without authority and stealing a motor vehicle.The 17-year old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his 14-year-old brother, Siddharth Aravind, inside their Martha Lane home on Tuesday before fleeing in his mother's car.Middlesex district attorney Marian Ryan and acton police chief Douglas Sturniolo said police received a call from teen's father shortly after 6.37 pm on August 11 after he was unable to contact his family. A tutor expected at the house had also been unable to reach anyone.The father had last spoken to Sudha early Tuesday morning before leaving for work, while Siddharth was last seen around noon, authorities said.Police who arrived at the house found both victims dead. Siddharth was found on the first floor and Sudha in the finished basement. Both victims were found with “obvious trauma”, but the chief medical examiner has yet to release information on the exact cause and manner of death.The type of weapon used in the killings is also still under investigation.The accused was not at the house when police arrived and was believed to have fled in his mother's vehicle. Investigators issued an alert for him as they searched for the teenager.He was found early Wednesday in the vehicle in a parking lot in Wayland, Massachusetts, after local police responded to an unrelated alarm. He was taken into custody without incident.The Middlesex county district attorney's office said investigators found that Arjun had recently displayed concerning behaviour."The subsequent investigation indicates that Arjun had recently been demonstrating concerning behaviour, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasies regarding killing his family,” the statement said.Arjun was expected to be arraigned in Lowell juvenile court on Wednesday. However, the juvenile court does not have jurisdiction over murder charges. He will therefore face arraignment on the murder and related assault charges in Concord district court later.
Article Summary: Indian-origin teenager charged with double murder of mother, brother in Massachusetts. The 17-year-old is accused of fatally assaulting his mother, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and his brother, Siddharth Aravind, 14. The teen has been charged with two counts of murder, two counts each of assault and battery.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates: "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually…" - a lesson on stepping outside your comfort zone
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates

Quote of the day by Melinda French Gates

"When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that"

Where this quote actually comes from

What the quote is actually saying

Why discomfort can genuinely be a sign of progress

Why stepping outside a comfort zone actually matters

Why failure is genuinely part of growth

Why real confidence tends to develop through experience, not before it

Why this idea applies directly to professional life

A note on Melinda French Gates

Other famous quotes by Melinda French Gates

"That is why we women have to lift each other up, not to replace men at the top of the hierarchy, but to become partners with men in ending hierarchy."

"I've never held the view that women are better than men, or that the best way to improve the world is for women to gain more power than men."

"Embrace change. Don't be afraid of it."

"I am simply not willing to accept that my granddaughters could grow up with less freedom than I did."

Why this quote continues to inspire people

Growth rarely feels comfortable while it is actually happening. Learning something new, taking on more responsibility, or simply stepping into an unfamiliar situation tends to bring real uncertainty along with it. Melinda French Gates put a name to that discomfort directly. "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that," she said. Rather than treating discomfort as an automatic warning sign, her point is that it often means something else entirely, that an old habit or a familiar limit is genuinely being challenged, and that the challenge itself is usually exactly where real growth actually happens. Her words encourage people to look at discomfort with greater curiosity, recognising that difficult moments can sometimes signal progress rather than failure or a reason to retreat. That practice of consciously reframing discomfort as evidence of growth, rather than a signal to retreat, reflects a deliberate mental habit French Gates has clearly cultivated over years of navigating unfamiliar and often high-pressure situations herself.French Gates said this in a Forbes interview with Marianne Schnall, published in April 2025, while discussing her memoir The Next Day, released the same year. She went further in the same conversation, describing exactly how she talks herself through discomfort in real time. "I'll literally coach myself in my head," she said. "'Okay, this is hard, but I must be growing here. It's going to be okay.' And then on the other side, you actually become far more resilient. " She added a piece of broader advice in the same interview too, "Embrace change. Don't be afraid of it... just know you've got a lot of tools inside of you." For French Gates, that mindset reflects the value of recognising difficult moments as opportunities to adapt, learn and develop greater confidence.Staying inside a comfort zone usually means staying inside the familiar, where there is less uncertainty and fewer situations that genuinely test existing ability. Growth tends to happen specifically once someone runs into something unfamiliar instead, a new responsibility that feels overwhelming, a moment of speaking up that feels intimidating, a new skill that feels frustrating at first. None of that discomfort is pleasant in the moment. It is often exactly what gradually expands what a person is actually capable of. This is why people who consistently seek out unfamiliar challenges tend to develop broader skill sets over time, while those who remain within familiar routines, however comfortable, often find their growth quietly stalling without ever fully realising it.Comfort usually comes from familiarity. When something feels uncomfortable, it often simply means someone has not fully mastered it yet, and that unfamiliarity is precisely what creates room to actually learn. A first attempt at something new is rarely smooth. Repeated effort is usually what eventually turns that uncertainty into real confidence, which is really how most skills get built in the first place.Comfort zones are not inherently a problem. They provide genuine stability and give people room to recover between challenges. The real issue starts once fear of discomfort stops someone trying anything new at all. Taking calculated steps beyond a familiar routine tends to expose people to new ideas and real opportunity, and over time, the boundaries of what actually feels comfortable start expanding on their own.Growth does not only happen through success. A mistake can reveal exactly where a real weakness sits. A difficult conversation can improve how someone communicates going forward. A rejected opportunity can push someone to prepare more thoroughly next time. Rather than treating every setback as proof of inadequacy, it can just as easily become useful information that helps someone actually improve.Confidence is not always something someone has to already possess before taking action. More often, it develops precisely because they took the action despite feeling genuinely uncertain about it. Each difficult experience becomes real evidence that a person can actually handle a challenge, and that evidence is what slowly builds resilience and self-belief over time.Career growth regularly requires people to take on responsibilities they have never handled before. A promotion might suddenly demand real leadership skill. A new job might involve completely unfamiliar systems. Avoiding those moments can feel comfortable in the short term, but it tends to limit development considerably further down the line, while embracing a reasonable challenge tends to open the door to real professional growth instead.Melinda French Gates is an American philanthropist, author and advocate who has worked extensively on global health, gender equality and women's economic empowerment. She co-founded the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, stepped away from it in 2024, and went on to lead Pivotal Ventures, an investment and incubation organisation she founded to advance social progress. Her 2019 book The Moment of Lift: How Empowering Women Changes the World explored many of these same themes at length.French Gates' words offer a genuinely simple way to rethink the moments that actually make people uncomfortable. Not every difficult experience is really a setback. Sometimes discomfort is exactly the evidence that someone is learning, adapting and becoming capable of something they genuinely could not do before. "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that" is really a reminder to approach unfamiliar experiences with curiosity rather than retreating from them immediately. Growth takes real patience, involves real mistakes, and often just requires the courage to stay in an uncomfortable situation long enough to actually learn something from it.
Article Summary: "When something's uncomfortable, it means you're actually growing, so embrace that" Melinda French Gates said this in a Forbes interview with Marianne Schnall, published in April 2025, while discussing her memoir The Next Day. French Gates has clearly cultivated over years of navigating unfamiliar and often high-pressure situations herself.

Article Title: Where is Bashar al-Assad? Ousted Syrian dictator sentenced to death in absentia
Article Text:
Synrian Ex-president Bashar Assad (2019 photo)

where is Bashar al-Assad now, and can Syria ever bring him back to face the punishment handed down by its court?

Assad remains in Russia after fleeing Syria

Where exactly in Moscow is Assad living?

Bashar Assad, left, and Russian President Vladimir Putin shake hands during their meeting in Moscow, Russia.

Russia has kept Assad away from public life

Why Syria sentenced Assad to death

Syria sentences absent Bashar al-Assad to death over killings and torture (Image: Reuters)

Verdict welcomed by Assad's victims

Can Syria actually bring Assad back?

From Syria's president to a secluded exile

Bashar al-Assad inherited his presidency from his father

A Syrian criminal court in Damascus has sentenced ousted president Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia after finding him guilty of killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and crimes against humanity committed during the country's nearly 14-year civil war. The verdict, delivered on Tuesday, August 11, marks the first conviction against Assad by Syria's transitional authorities since his regime collapsed in December 2024. But while the court has pronounced a death sentence, the former Syrian ruler remains far beyond the reach of the authorities who now control Damascus.Assad is currently in Russia, where he and his family were granted asylum after fleeing Syria when rebel forces captured Damascus in December 2024. His precise location inside Russia has not been publicly confirmed. However, reporting over the past year has placed the former dictator in Moscow, with sources previously indicating that his family was likely living in the heavily guarded Rublyovka area, an affluent district on the western outskirts of the Russian capital.The death sentence therefore raises a central question:The most recent credible reports continue to place Assad in Moscow.Reuters reported after Tuesday's verdict that Assad "is currently in Russia", where he and his family received asylum on humanitarian grounds. His brother Maher al-Assad, who also received a death sentence in absentia, is likewise believed to be in Russia.Assad's escape from Syria came on December 8, 2024, when rebel forces led by Ahmed al-Sharaa swept into Damascus after a lightning offensive that lasted less than two weeks. The advance brought down the Assad government and ended more than five decades of rule by the Assad family.At the time, Assad's whereabouts were initially unknown. Russia's foreign ministry said he had resigned and left Syria, while reports suggested he had travelled from the coastal region before being flown to Russia. Russian state media subsequently reported that Assad and his family had arrived in Moscow and had been granted asylum.In a statement issued after his escape, Assad disputed accounts that he had planned his departure in advance. He said he had remained in Damascus until the final hours and later moved to a Russian military base in Latakia as the security situation deteriorated."First, my departure from Syria was neither planned nor did it occur during the final hours of the battles, as some have claimed," Assad said in the statement."On the contrary, I remained in Damascus, carrying out my duties until the early hours of Sunday, December 8, 2024," he added.According to Assad's account, he travelled to the Russian Khmeimim airbase in Latakia after opposition forces entered Damascus and intended to continue overseeing military operations. He said the situation at the base then became untenable and Moscow asked its command to arrange his evacuation."With no viable means of leaving the base, Moscow requested that the base's command arrange an immediate evacuation to Russia on the evening of Sunday 8 December," the statement said.Independent reporting has also described Assad's departure as a Russian-assisted evacuation. The Guardian reported in December 2025 that Assad and his sons were taken under Russian military escort to Khmeimim before being flown out of Syria.This is where the trail becomes less certain. There is no publicly verified address for Assad in Moscow, and he has rarely, if ever, been seen publicly since arriving in Russia. A detailed Guardian investigation published in December 2025, based on sources in Russia and Syria, a family friend and leaked data, reported that the Assad family was likely living in Rublyovka, a prestigious gated area associated with Russia's political and business elite.The report described the family's life in Moscow as secluded and closely controlled. A family friend said Assad had little contact with the outside world and remained in touch with only a small number of people who had served around his presidential palace."It's a very quiet life," said the family friend. "He has very little, if any, contact with the outside world. He's only in touch with a couple of people who were in his palace, like Mansour Azzam [former Syrian minister of presidency affairs] and Yassar Ibrahim [Assad's top economic crony]."The same investigation said Assad was studying Russian and revisiting his training in ophthalmology. Before entering politics, Assad had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and had originally intended to pursue a medical career before the death of his elder brother Basil changed the succession plans of the Assad family."He’s studying Russian and brushing up on his ophthalmology again," a family friend told the Guardian. "It’s a passion of his, he obviously doesn’t need the money. Even before the war in Syria began, he used to regularly practice his ophthalmology in Damascus."However, the Rublyovka location should be treated as a reported possibility rather than a confirmed current address. What is firmly established is that Assad remains in Russia and has been kept away from public political life.Moscow's decision to shelter Assad has been one of the biggest obstacles to attempts by Syria's new authorities to bring the former president before a court.Russia granted Assad and his family asylum on humanitarian grounds after the fall of his government. Since then, reports have indicated that the Kremlin has placed restrictions on his public activities.In a November 2025 interview cited by the Guardian, Russia's ambassador to Iraq, Elbrus Kutrashev, said Assad was safe in Russia but could not engage in political or media activity."Assad may live here but cannot engage in political activities … He has no right to engage in any media or political activity. Have you heard anything from him? You haven’t, because he is not allowed to – but he is safe and alive," Kutrashev said.The restrictions have contributed to the mystery surrounding Assad's life in exile. Unlike other deposed leaders who have appeared publicly after leaving office, Assad has remained largely invisible.His children, however, have had a somewhat more visible life in Moscow. The Guardian reported that Assad's daughter Zein attended the prestigious Moscow State Institute of International Relations, known as MGIMO, and graduated in June 2025. Other family members were also seen at the ceremony, although they kept a low profile.The family has also reportedly travelled to the United Arab Emirates, a destination with which it had longstanding connections. But reports said the family initially hoped to relocate there permanently and later concluded that such a move would be difficult because of the political implications of hosting Assad.The Damascus court's verdict is the first Syrian conviction against Assad himself. The court found him guilty of offences including premeditated and intentional murder, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity. His younger brother Maher was handed the same sentence in absentia.Maher commanded Syria's elite Fourth Armoured Division and was one of the most powerful military figures under Assad. The division was repeatedly accused by opposition activists and rights groups of involvement in crackdowns, killings and torture during the conflict.Assad's cousin Atef Najib, the former head of political security in Deraa province, was also sentenced to death. Unlike Assad and Maher, Najib was in Syrian custody and appeared in court wearing a prison uniform.Najib's role is particularly important because Deraa is widely regarded as the birthplace of the 2011 uprising against Assad. The unrest began after security forces detained and allegedly tortured teenagers who had written anti-government graffiti on a school wall.The crackdown that followed helped turn local protests into nationwide demonstrations. The government's violent response contributed to the escalation into an armed conflict that eventually drew in regional and global powers.The court also sentenced several other former military and security officials to death in absentia, including former defence minister Fahd al-Freij and former military intelligence chief in Deraa Louay al-Ali.The ruling was met with celebrations in parts of Syria, particularly in areas that suffered heavily under Assad's security forces.Crowds gathered outside the courthouse in Damascus, chanting and waving Syrian flags. In Deraa, families of people killed or detained during the early years of the uprising gathered with photographs of their relatives.For many victims, the verdict carried significance beyond the punishment itself. It was an official acknowledgement by Syria's new authorities of crimes committed during the Assad era.Noha al-Masri, a prosecutor involved in the case, lost her brother during the crackdown in Deraa in 2011."We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us," Masri told the BBC."Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."Reuters reported that the trial process lasted nearly four months and was presented by Syria's new authorities as part of a wider effort to pursue transitional justice after the fall of Assad.But the verdict has also drawn criticism from human rights groups over the fairness of the proceedings. The Associated Press reported that rights organisations raised concerns about whether the trials were rushed and whether defendants received adequate legal protections. Human Rights Watch also criticised the use of the death penalty, saying accountability requires a justice system capable of guaranteeing fair trials.For now, the answer appears to be no. The death sentence has no immediate practical effect on Assad because he is outside Syrian territory and under Russian protection. Syria would need Russia to surrender him or otherwise allow him to be transferred to Syrian custody.Anwar al-Bunni, head of the Syrian Centre for Legal Studies and Research, argued that the death sentence itself could make extradition harder."There is a huge problem, which is that no one will hand over a criminal to a country that issues a death sentence. This will cut off the road to Assad, and many other criminals, being handed over to Syria," Bunni told Reuters."This is performative justice, not transitional justice," he said.Syria's new authorities have previously sought accountability for Assad and senior figures from his government. The issue has also been part of the complicated relationship between Damascus and Moscow. Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa travelled to Moscow in October 2025 for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Assad's extradition among the issues surrounding the relationship.Assad also faces legal action outside Syria. France has issued an arrest warrant against him over allegations connected to the bombing of a press centre in Homs in 2012, according to Reuters.Assad inherited the presidency in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez al-Assad, who had ruled Syria for nearly three decades. Bashar initially presented himself as a modernising leader, but his rule became increasingly associated with political repression and the security apparatus.The defining event of his presidency was the 2011 uprising. What began as protests demanding political change developed into a devastating civil war involving the Syrian government, opposition groups, extremist organisations and foreign powers. Russia intervened militarily in support of Assad in 2015, helping his forces regain territory and eventually reducing the opposition's hold over much of the country.For years, Assad appeared to have survived the war. Then, in late 2024, the balance changed with extraordinary speed.Forces led by Ahmed al-Sharaa launched an offensive from northern Syria and advanced rapidly towards Damascus. On December 8, the capital fell and the Assad government collapsed.The man who had ruled Syria for more than two decades disappeared from the country and resurfaced in Moscow.Nearly two years later, a Syrian court has sentenced him to death. Yet the most important fact remains unchanged: Bashar al-Assad is not in a Syrian prison. He is in Russia, living under the protection of the country that stood by his regime during the civil war.His exact whereabouts in Moscow remain undisclosed. Reports have pointed to the elite Rublyovka district, while other details of his life suggest a tightly controlled existence away from politics and public view.The Damascus verdict therefore closes one chapter of Assad's rule, but not the question of whether the former Syrian president will ever return to the country he ruled for 24 years.For now, the death sentence exists on paper in Damascus while Assad remains thousands of kilometres away in Russia.
Article Summary: Bashar al-Assad was sentenced to death in absentia by a Syrian court. He was found guilty of killings, torture, arbitrary arrests and crimes against humanity. Assad fled Syria when rebel forces captured Damascus in December 2024. He and his family were granted asylum in Russia, where they are believed to be living.

Article Title: How Iranian missile threat sparked a secret operation to move Trump out of Turkey as Air Force One flew as a decoy
Article Text:
President Donald Trump holds a press conference during the Nato summit in Ankara, Turkey

US President Donald Trump was secretly moved out of Turkey aboard a smaller military aircraft after American officials received intelligence about a possible Iranian assassination threat during the Nato summit in Ankara.“The threat was serious enough that extreme measures needed to be taken that day,” a US official told CNN, describing the decision by the Secret Service to take extraordinary precautions despite uncertainty over the intelligence.The warning reportedly indicated that Iranian actors knew the luxury hotel where Trump was staying, had information about his movements in Ankara and remained intent on killing him. US officials also received intelligence about a possible attack on Air Force One using a shoulder fired missile launched from the ground near Ankara airport.The intelligence had been shared by Israel with the CIA. However, the warning was not universally accepted within the US administration. Some CIA officials questioned its credibility and whether Iran had the capability to carry out such an attack, CNN reported.US intelligence assessments before Trump's Turkey trip had not indicated a new, specific Iranian plot to assassinate the president. Instead, officials had been monitoring continuing threats and chatter from Iranian actors calling for Trump's death.The missile warning nevertheless triggered a rapidly evolving security assessment on July 8, with senior US officials working alongside the Secret Service to determine how Trump could safely leave Turkey.General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, was among the senior officials involved in the discussions at the heavily fortified Bestepe Presidential Complex. Some officials initially considered taking Trump out of Turkey earlier in the day, but that option was rejected and the president continued his scheduled meetings.Trump later held his Nato summit press conference, where he acknowledged the danger surrounding him and said he was on “every single one” of Iran's lists.Trump had arrived in Turkey aboard the Qatar donated Boeing 747 that he had promoted as the future Air Force One. He had previously told Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan that the older presidential aircraft was now only the “back-up”.Trump later posted that the Qatar donated aircraft would fly to a British airbase so troops could tour it, while he would take the older Air Force One back to the United States. In reality, Trump would take neither aircraft.The plan required him to board the older Air Force One before secretly moving through another exit into a white catering truck parked alongside the aircraft. The truck had been emptied and cleaned earlier in the day after US officials arranged to use it.Trump, along with executive assistant Natalie Harp, Oval Office operations director Walt Nauta, White House personnel chief Dan Scavino and Secret Service agents, were placed inside the truck.The vehicle took 162 seconds to cross the airport tarmac before reaching a smaller C-32A aircraft. Defense secretary Pete Hegseth also joined Trump aboard the military aircraft for the flight to RAF Mildenhall in Britain.Meanwhile, several senior officials remained aboard the larger Air Force One, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Some White House staff and journalists were reportedly unaware that Trump was no longer aboard the aircraft and were instructed to keep the window shades closed.The operation effectively turned Air Force One into a decoy while Trump travelled aboard the C-32A.Fighter jets were reportedly prepared to escort both aircraft out of Turkey, suggesting that US officials remained concerned about the possibility of an attack even after Trump had been moved to the smaller aircraft.CNN reported that no militants were arrested and no evidence of a missile plot was recovered after Trump left Turkey. The precise source of the intelligence about the shoulder fired missile also remains unclear.The episode highlights the difficult calculations involved in protecting a US president. Even though some officials doubted the intelligence and questioned whether Iran could execute such an attack, the potential consequences of being wrong were considered serious enough to justify an elaborate deception involving a catering truck, a secret aircraft and a decoy Air Force One.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump was secretly moved out of Turkey aboard a smaller military aircraft. American officials received intelligence about a possible Iranian assassination threat during the Nato summit in Ankara. The warning indicated that Iranian actors knew the luxury hotel where Trump was staying, had information about his movements in Ankara and remained intent on killing him. US officials also received information about possible attack on Air Force One using a shoulder fired missile.

Article Title: Sniper, knife, missile threats: Israel warned US of alleged Iran plot to assassinate Donald Trump
Article Text:
Israel warned US of sniper, knife, missile threats against Trump; White House says could not verify. (Benjamin Netanyahu, Donald Trump)

CIA had low confidence in some Israeli intelligence

Turkey found no evidence to corroborate warning

Intelligence-sharing tensions inside US administration
