Israel warned the United States over several alleged Iranian plots to assassinate President Donald Trump, including possible sniper, knife and shoulder-launched missile attacks, but US intelligence agencies could not independently verify the specific threats, according to Reuters report quoting current and former US officials .The warnings were passed to US intelligence agencies and, in some cases, directly to senior White House officials, with the most detailed alert coming ahead of Trump's trip to Turkey for the Nato summit in July. Despite the lack of verification, the White House and Secret Service took precautionary measures, including moving Trump from Air Force One to another aircraft during the trip.The warnings began before the 12-day war in June 2025 and intensified ahead of the US decision to go to war with Iran in February, according to the sources.The most detailed warning came ahead of the Nato summit in Ankara in July, when Israeli officials told the White House that Iran could try to kill Trump while he travelled aboard Air Force One, potentially using a shoulder-launched missile, the US official and another person familiar with the matter said.Despite the lack of independent verification, the warnings prompted the White House and Secret Service to take additional precautions.During Trump's Turkey trip, the Secret Service carried out an unusual deception operation by moving him from Air Force One to another aircraft for his flight out of the country, according to the sources.The US intelligence community has long assessed that Iran wants to retaliate against Trump over the 2020 US drone strike that killed Iranian military commander Qassem Soleimani. However, the CIA has been unable to corroborate some of the specific threats against Trump's life shared by Israeli intelligence since early last year, the officials said.In several instances during the two US military offensives against Iran, the CIA assessed that it had "low confidence" in Israeli intelligence concerning threats posed by Iran, including alleged plans to assassinate Trump, according to one former US official and another person familiar with the matter.It remained unclear how widely those assessments had circulated within the Trump administration.The warnings also exposed broader differences between US and Israeli intelligence assessments on Iran. Earlier this year, US intelligence agencies assessed that Iran was not actively building a nuclear weapon, while Israel maintained that Tehran posed an urgent threat.Trump nevertheless proceeded with strikes against Iran in February. Reuters had previously reported that intelligence shared by Israel about alleged Iranian attempts to assassinate Trump was among the information he considered before launching the military campaign.A spokesperson for the Israeli embassy rejected the suggestion that Israel was using intelligence to influence US policy towards Iran."The same people who claim that Israel is trying to influence US policy through alleged intelligence sharing would just as soon accuse Israel of concealing critical information if it benefited their own agenda," the spokesperson said.Secret Service spokesman Anthony Guglielmi also declined to discuss specific intelligence matters, but said the agency remained focused on protecting Trump amid recent assassination attempts and increased threats against the president."The U.S. Secret Service continuously analyzes a wide range of information to guide our protective operations in real time and across every location we secure," he said.Also read: How Iranian missile threat sparked a secret operation to move Trump out of Turkey as Air Force One flew as a decoy The alleged threat during Trump's Turkey trip was not independently corroborated by Turkish intelligence, according to a Turkish official.The official said Turkey's intelligence agencies had no evidence supporting the Israeli warning that Iran intended to target Trump and that the assessment was shared with US officials.The episode nevertheless demonstrated the extent to which Israeli intelligence was shaping security decisions around Trump at a time of heightened tensions with Tehran.The United States has long relied heavily on Israeli intelligence on Middle East issues, particularly concerning Iran. Israeli intelligence typically reaches the CIA or National Security Agency through formal channels before being assessed alongside other intelligence, according to two former US officials.US agencies often cannot independently verify Israeli intelligence but use other information to assess its authenticity and accuracy, the officials said.The Israeli warnings also came amid changes in how intelligence assessments were being produced within the Trump administration.Two former US officials said senior Israeli officials and representatives had contacted the White House on several occasions over the past year, including through the Situation Room, to brief senior Trump officials directly about Iranian threats.Such direct engagement has occurred amid a broader breakdown in intelligence-sharing arrangements within the US administration.Last year, amid rising tensions with the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the CIA stopped working on joint assessments with the National Intelligence Council, according to the former officials.The National Intelligence Council is the US intelligence community's senior analytical body and is overseen by the ODNI. It produces assessments intended to reflect the broader intelligence community's view, with the CIA serving as its largest contributor.Recent Iran assessments by the council have also declined partly because of layoffs at the ODNI, according to the officials and another person familiar with the matter. The NSA declined to comment.
Article Summary: Israel warned US of sniper, knife, missile threats against Trump; White House says could not verify. CIA had "low confidence" in Israeli intelligence concerning threats posed by Iran, including alleged plans to assassinate Trump. The most detailed warning came ahead of the Nato summit in Ankara in July, when Israeli officials said Iran could try to kill Trump.

Article Title: In 1970, a Missouri family fought the government over nearly 600 acres wanted for a national park; an initial $73,000 offer became a $214,000 court payout
Article Text:
The Blackwell family, with Amanda in the front and, standing behind her from left to right, Brad, Scott, Shelia and Darrel.

The Blackwell family’s farm along Current River

From a family farm to a national park

The $73,000 offer that became $214,000

Darrel worked for the National Park Service while his father fought it

Darrel witnessed the dedication of Ozark National Scenic Riverways

From farming and teaching to canoe rentals

A life intertwined with the Riverways

A rare connection to Ozark National Scenic Riverways

In 1970, a Missouri farming family found itself at the centre of a legal battle with the federal government after officials sought to acquire nearly 600 acres of its land for the creation of a new national park.The Blackwell family farm, known as the “Blackwell Tract”, sat across from Pulltite along the Current River in northern Shannon County. According to an article published by the National Park Service’s Ozark National Scenic Riverways, the government initially offered the family $73,000 for the property. After the case went to federal court, the Blackwells ultimately received $214,000 for nearly 600 acres.The story is closely tied to Darrel Blackwell, who went on to have a unique relationship with the National Park Service. He worked as a seasonal park ranger during the early years of Ozark National Scenic Riverways, while his father was simultaneously fighting the agency in court over the family’s farm. Years later, Darrel became a concessioner for the park through Jadwin Canoe Rental.Darrel grew up in Rector, Missouri, with his father Wayne, mother Iceline and brother Charlie. Wayne was a farmer who managed two properties - one in Rector and another along the Current River across from what is now Pulltite.Wayne purchased the Current River farm in the mid-1930s. In 1937, he and Roy Weise built a road down to Pulltite to improve access to the property. The route of that early road is now largely followed by Highway EE.The family’s farming operation centred primarily on cattle, although crops were also grown for a time in the bottom fields along the river.As the farm expanded, Wayne acquired two additional tracts of land. The family also employed caretakers who lived permanently on the property and helped manage the growing agricultural operation.The Blackwell farm eventually became one of the properties acquired by the federal government during the establishment of Ozark National Scenic Riverways.The park, which protects portions of the Current and Jacks Fork rivers in Missouri, was created to preserve the rivers and the surrounding natural and cultural resources.Darrel recalled that his father did not initially receive an offer for the property.“When the government came to buy my dad’s place, they didn’t offer him anything for it,” Darrel said, according to the National Park Service account. “They told him they were going to use the power of eminent domain to condemn the property and they would have to go to court.”Wayne accepted that the government had the legal authority to pursue eminent domain but wanted the family to receive what he considered a fair price for the land.The legal dispute came to a head in 1970, when the acquisition was finalized.Darrel recalled that his father hired Dorman Steelman, another Current River resident, but because the attorney could not practice in federal court, the family brought in another lawyer from Cape Girardeau.“The government originally offered us $73,000 for the farm,” Darrel recalled.The case then went before a federal court to determine the value of the property.One unusual moment during the proceedings involved Darrel’s mother, Iceline. According to Darrel, she carried candy in her purse and was caught handing some to members of the jury during a recess.“Mom always had a purse with some candy in it,” Darrel recalled. “During a recess from the proceedings, she was caught handing out candy to members of the jury members.”The judge intervened and told her she could not do so, although Darrel said it was clear she meant no harm.After the proceedings, the family received $214,000 for “right at 600 acres” - substantially more than the government’s initial $73,000 offer.Perhaps the most unusual part of Darrel’s story is that he was working for the very agency his father was battling in court.Darrel served as a seasonal park ranger from 1969 to 1972, during the same period his father was fighting the National Park Service over the family farm.He said his father did not object to him working for the agency.Darrel remembered his years as a ranger fondly, describing the job as one where every day brought something different. Rangers patrolled the river by canoe and horseback, looked after campgrounds, assisted visitors and provided information.He also recalled that public safety and helping visitors were central to the job, with law enforcement considered a secondary responsibility.Darrel was also among the park employees present for the dedication ceremony for Ozark National Scenic Riverways in 1972 at Big Spring.Tricia Nixon, daughter of then-President Richard Nixon, attended the ceremony.Darrel recalled being assigned to escort her toward the spring and keep photographers from getting too close.He remembered the moment vividly, particularly her appearance and the hectic atmosphere surrounding the event.His experience meant that Darrel had been connected to Ozark National Scenic Riverways from several different perspectives — as the son of a landowner whose property was acquired for the park, as a park ranger and eventually as a business operator serving visitors to the Riverways.After leaving the park service, Darrel increasingly turned his attention to tourism and outdoor recreation.In the fall of 1972, he partnered with Jack Peters and John Hambacker to purchase Camp Zoe, a youth camp located at the site of what is now Echo Bluff State Park.A few months later, in January 1973, Darrel purchased Jadwin Canoe Rental from Clinton and Sue Jadwin.The canoe rental business eventually became the centre of his professional life.Darrel initially operated from a farmhouse at the junction of Highway K and Highway ZZ. In 1977, he purchased the building where Jadwin Canoe Rental currently operates, which had previously served as a local grocery store.His early transportation methods were equally unconventional. The business initially used Suburbans to transport visitors, but Darrel recalled that customers were sometimes taken to the river in the back of a stock truck.He later expanded the operation, including purchasing a 1967 Chevrolet 48-passenger bus in 1975.Darrel eventually spent decades running Jadwin Canoe Rental, building a life and business around the visitors coming to the Ozarks.He said the most important part of the business was not the equipment itself but the way customers were treated.“If you don’t provide a quality service for visitors the first time, they won’t ever come back,” Darrel said. “The only thing that separates one from another is how you treat your customers and how you take care of your customers.”For him, the canoe rental business became much more than a job. He said it allowed him to make a living with the help of his wife, who worked as a schoolteacher, while remaining connected to the people and landscape he had known throughout his life.“I’ve enjoyed it,” Darrel said. “I have a great wife, I have three wonderful kids, and I have three beautiful grandkids.”The National Park Service describes Darrel Blackwell as a one-of-a-kind figure because of his three distinct connections to Ozark National Scenic Riverways.He worked as a park ranger during the park’s early years, his family’s farm was acquired through eminent domain during the park’s creation, and he later became a National Park Service concessioner through Jadwin Canoe Rental.Those experiences placed Darrel on both sides of the park’s early history - first as part of a family whose land was taken for its creation, then as an employee of the agency responsible for managing it, and finally as a business owner whose livelihood depended on the visitors drawn to the Riverways.
Article Summary: Darrel Blackwell grew up in Rector, Missouri, with his father Wayne, mother Iceline and brother Charlie. Wayne was a farmer who managed two properties - one in. Rector and another along the Current River across from what is now Pulltite. The family’s farming operation centred primarily on cattle, although crops were also grown for a time in the bottom fields along the river. As the farm expanded, Wayne acquired two additional tracts of land.

Article Title: Quote of the day by CT Fletcher: "Everything is impossible, until someone crazy enough comes along and…" - a lesson in persistence and unconventional thinking
Article Text:
Quote of the day by CT Fletcher (Image source: Instagram/c.t.ali.fletcher)

Quote of the day by CT Fletcher

"Everything is impossible, until someone crazy enough comes along and makes it possible"

Meaning and interpretation of CT Fletcher's quote

Why "impossible" so often changes over time

Why unconventional thinkers actually matter

The real role persistence plays here

Why other people's doubt can quietly become a real barrier

Why "crazy enough" was never really about being reckless

How to apply CT Fletcher’s lesson in daily life

Question the limits you have accepted : Ask whether something is genuinely impossible or simply difficult, unfamiliar or yet to be achieved.

: Ask whether something is genuinely impossible or simply difficult, unfamiliar or yet to be achieved. Try a different approach : If the usual method is not working, consider whether changing the approach could produce a different result.

: If the usual method is not working, consider whether changing the approach could produce a different result. Do not confuse criticism with fact : Other people's doubts can sometimes highlight genuine problems, but they do not automatically prove that a goal cannot be achieved.

: Other people's doubts can sometimes highlight genuine problems, but they do not automatically prove that a goal cannot be achieved. Learn from failure : An unsuccessful attempt can show what needs to change rather than proving that the entire goal is impossible.

: An unsuccessful attempt can show what needs to change rather than proving that the entire goal is impossible. Stay persistent but practical : Persistence works best when it is combined with preparation, learning and a willingness to adapt.

: Persistence works best when it is combined with preparation, learning and a willingness to adapt. Start with one achievable step: Even a huge goal becomes easier to approach when it is broken into smaller tasks that can be acted upon.

Other memorable quotes by CT Fletcher

"History never remembers the haters."

"I command you to grow!"

"Pain is necessary, embrace the pain!"

"Will is the key to success. Remember who you are and don't let nobody tell you that you can't do it."

Why this quote by CT Fletcher remains relevant today

What seems impossible is often simply something that has not actually been achieved yet. CT Fletcher, the powerlifter and motivational speaker known for his intense workout videos, captured that idea directly. "Everything is impossible, until someone crazy enough comes along and makes it possible," he said. The word "crazy" here is not really about irrational behaviour. It describes someone genuinely willing to challenge accepted limits and keep pursuing an idea even when conventional thinking insists it simply cannot be done. Fletcher himself is a fairly striking example of the idea in action, a former US Army serviceman who took up weightlifting in his twenties and went on to become a world champion powerlifter, later building an entirely unexpected second career from viral videos of his own intense training sessions well into his sixties, long after most people assume that particular chapter of a person's life has already closed.The quote suggests that impossibility is sometimes a genuinely temporary judgement rather than a fixed, permanent fact. Throughout history, people have attempted things that initially looked completely unrealistic. Before the first successful flight, powered human flight seemed impossible to most people. Before humans ever reached the Moon, the idea of leaving Earth and travelling there largely belonged to science fiction.Whoever eventually succeeds usually has to be willing to question the exact assumptions that made a goal look impossible in the first place.The actual meaning of impossible is not always fixed in place. Something can be genuinely impossible given the technology, knowledge or resources available at a specific moment, and as those conditions shift, the exact same challenge can suddenly become achievable. Human progress is full of examples of this pattern. A new discovery can turn a previously unsolvable problem into something closer to a practical engineering challenge. The quote really connects ambition directly with progress. Someone has to be willing to attempt the very first step before anyone else can see that something is genuinely achievable at all.People who challenge established ideas are not always immediately understood by everyone around them. An unconventional approach can look genuinely strange simply because it does not follow the familiar method, but questioning established assumptions can sometimes reveal real possibilities that a conventional approach overlooks entirely. This does not mean every unconventional idea turns out to be correct. Real experimentation still requires evidence, planning and genuine persistence. The genuinely useful part is the willingness to ask whether the existing limits are actually fixed at all.An ambitious idea rarely becomes reality after just one attempt. Failure can reveal genuine weaknesses in the original approach and provide real information for whatever comes next. Persistence is what lets a person adjust their approach rather than abandoning the entire goal immediately. This matters enormously when working toward something that genuinely has not been achieved before, since there may be no established formula for success available anywhere. The person actually attempting it has to learn as they go.People often judge a new idea entirely according to what they already know. If something has genuinely never been done successfully before, it can be genuinely difficult to imagine how it might actually work. That can produce real scepticism, harsh criticism or outright dismissal. Sometimes that criticism identifies a genuine problem worth addressing. At other times, it simply reflects the limits of current understanding at the time. The real challenge lies in learning to tell useful criticism apart from assumptions that genuinely deserve to be questioned.Fletcher's wording is deliberately provocative, but pursuing a genuinely ambitious goal does not actually require ignoring reality. Turning an apparently impossible idea into something possible usually involves real experimentation, careful preparation, genuine technical knowledge and repeated refinement over time. The person who eventually succeeds might look "crazy" simply for attempting the goal in the first place, but the actual process behind the achievement is usually considerably more disciplined than the initial idea ever suggested. Courage and preparation can genuinely exist together.Every generation runs into problems that look genuinely too difficult to solve at first. The instinctive reaction is often to look directly at the existing limits and simply conclude the goal cannot be reached. Fletcher's quote encourages a different question instead, what if that limit has simply never actually been tested by someone genuinely willing to challenge it. That does not mean every impossible-looking goal can actually be achieved. Some real limitations genuinely are fixed. Progress still tends to depend on people willing to actually investigate whether a supposed limitation is really permanent, and the person who attempts something everyone else dismisses may fail repeatedly along the way. If the attempt eventually succeeds regardless, what once looked completely impossible can quickly become the new ordinary standard, which is exactly the pattern Fletcher himself lived out on his own path from Army serviceman to genuine world champion.
Article Summary: "Everything is impossible, until someone crazy enough comes along and makes it possible" is the quote of the day by powerlifter and motivational speaker CT Fletcher. The quote suggests that impossibility is sometimes a genuinely temporary judgement rather than a fixed, permanent fact.

Article Title: In 1962, New Jersey took a family's seaside property through eminent domain for a new park; they challenged the price and were awarded $350,000
Article Text:
Photos courtesy NPS/Gateway NRA

Early ship tracking and radio experiments

How the Navesink lighthouses worked

Changes to the landscape and ice harvesting

A collection of vintage postcards donated to the National Park Service has given historians a detailed look at life along the New Jersey coast in the early 20th century.In a series of oral history interviews conducted by National Park Service historians Tom Hoffman and Elaine Harmon, retired Lieutenant Colonel John Joseph Patrick Mulhern examined items from the Paul Koeptchem postcard collection. He shared memories of living and working on the Sandy Hook peninsula between 1908 and 1927.The collection contains 24 colour postcards, catalogued as series number 272 at the Sandy Hook museum. It entered the National Park Service archives in November 1975 after Emily Tepia, the executor of Koeptchem’s estate, donated it. Koeptchem lived in Highland Beach from 1907 until 1962.The interview transcript, published by the National Park Service as part of the Gateway National Recreation Area’s historical records, shows how coastal communities and maritime stations operated before modern navigation technology and large-scale development.While looking at a postcard showing the Twin Lights of Navesink, Mulhern explained how ships were tracked along the New Jersey coast before electronic tracking systems existed.According to his account, marine observers working for commercial telecommunications companies watched ships heading toward New York Harbor from towers along the coast.“All these men, marine observers kept 3 x 5 cards on which they had manually prepared the silhouettes of all known vessels that would come in and out of New York Harbor,” Mulhern said in the interview.The observers could identify ships by features such as the number of smokestacks, masts, and the overall shape of the vessel. They also knew when certain ships were expected and could report their movements as they passed specific points on the way into New York Harbor.Mulhern also remembered his own connection to early radio technology. In 1919, he and Earl Lucas, the son of Twin Lights keeper Earl Lucas, obtained amateur radio licences together.Lucas placed an antenna between the lighthouse’s north and south towers. This helped launch a long career in radio engineering, eventually leading to his position as chief engineer at station WPAT.Mulhern also identified landmarks in the postcard images, including the anchors of an early Marconi wireless tower just north of the north lighthouse. The anchors were still visible in the ground decades later.The oral history also explains how the Twin Lights operated in the early 1900s.Although the site had two towers, Mulhern said only the south tower normally operated as a navigation light.“The lighthouses, as long as I can remember there was only one operational light and that was the one at the south end of this structure,” he said in the National Park Service transcript.The south light used a revolving double convex lens. A clock-like mechanical system turned the heavy glass lens.The system was powered by a large weight that slowly dropped and had to be manually wound back up once or more each day. The mechanism powered both the clockwork and the rotating lens.To people standing close to the lighthouse on land, the light appeared steady. But sailors about 15 miles offshore saw a fast flashing light as the lens turned.The north tower used a fixed light. It mainly served as a backup when the main south light was being repaired or maintained.Mulhern also recalled that visitors could enter the lighthouse only when the keeper allowed them to. It was not operated as a public park at the time.Later, federal officials added notes to nautical charts identifying the light as privately maintained. This helped protect shipowners from making claims against state authorities if a vessel ran aground, especially as newer technologies such as Loran and radar replaced traditional lighthouse navigation.While reviewing postcards of the Highland Beach resort, which was operated by the Sandlass family from 1893 to 1962, Mulhern pointed out changes to the peninsula’s landscape and buildings.The postcards show open fields, empty lots, and freshwater ponds that have since been replaced by homes and paved roads. During Mulhern’s childhood, these natural areas were important parts of everyday life.“In fact, some of them are built right on top of the spot where there used to be ponds where we used to go ice skating in the wintertime,” Mulhern recalled in the National Park Service record.He also explained that ice was cut from the ponds during winter and sold to nearby homes or stored in icehouses.Mulhern remembered how transportation changed across the peninsula. Before permanent roads were built, people travelled over the sandy ground using wooden trestles and gravel roads.Before modern highways, flatcars and horse-drawn wagons travelled beneath railway trestles near the Sandlass Bathing House. The area’s first single-lane concrete road was built around 1916 or 1917 during the First World War period.The postcard collection and oral history transcripts remain part of the permanent historical reference library at Gateway National Recreation Area. Together, they provide valuable primary-source evidence about the region’s maritime activities, technology, communities, and changing landscape.
Article Summary: The collection contains 24 colour postcards, catalogued as series number 272 at the Sandy Hook museum. It entered the National Park Service archives in November 1975 after Emily Tepia, the executor of Paul Koeptchem’s estate, donated it.

Article Title: Mohuya Khan, 27, made about $130,000 from nine income streams in 2025 while living in Queens; after taxes and expenses, she took home about $70,000
Article Text:
Native New Yorker Mohuya Khan, 27, in her apartment in Astoria, Queens. Lucia Vazquez for BI

Early career and financial struggles

Managing costs in Astoria

Setting healthier work boundaries

Operating nine different income streams from her one-bedroom apartment in Astoria, Queens, 27-year-old content creator and business owner Mohuya Khan generated about $130,000 in gross revenue in 2025.After business expenses and taxes, Khan kept about $70,000 in take-home income, according to financial details shared with Business Insider for its “Cost of the City” series, which follows people dealing with the high cost of living in major U.S. cities.Although Khan has achieved financial independence and has no debt, she said managing nine sources of income while working long hours pushed her close to physical and mental exhaustion.“Living in New York City, it’s kind of a double-edged sword,” Khan told Business Insider. “You see, everyone, for the most part, around you hustling. You see people working multiple jobs, and obviously they’re tired, but they’re just doing it because it’s kind of the normal way of living here.”Khan was born in Queens to Bangladeshi immigrant parents. Watching her parents work long hours taught her the importance of hard work from an early age.Her father drove a New York City taxi for 16 hours a day, seven days a week. Her mother encouraged her to work harder than others if she wanted to achieve her goals.Khan got her first job at 15, earned her driver’s licence at 16, and moved into her own apartment at 22 while attending college. She earned her undergraduate degree from Hunter College and later studied childhood education there.To pay for school and living costs without depending on others, she worked as an after-school counsellor while using student loans and personal savings.During the pandemic, Khan began posting her artwork on YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok. As her audience grew, she used tutorials on YouTube and Skillshare to improve her illustration skills.She eventually left her education career and started her own fashion brand, Labyrinthave, which combines Indo-Western and Bangladeshi design influences.When she first became self-employed full time, Khan depended on her savings and determination. However, she now warns others not to leave a stable job without enough financial security.“I don’t recommend everyone just to quit your job, and just work on your passions,” Khan told Business Insider. “It sounds great on paper, but when you try to actually do it, and you don’t have money saved up or a stable job or income that is going to come in, it is so scary to not have that.”Looking back, she said the period was extremely demanding and that she had few personal boundaries.“I’m proud of her, but I don’t know if I would do it again,” she said. “It motivated me. It also really burned me out.”Khan now shares a $3,000 monthly rent for her Astoria apartment with her husband.Her regular expenses include utilities, which cost between $50 and $210 a month depending on heating and cooling needs. Groceries for two people cost up to $400 each month.Khan owns a car and pays $300 a month for insurance. However, the vehicle stays at her parents’ home so her mother can use it. Khan usually travels around New York using the subway.She also uses some of her income to help her parents pay their mortgage. In addition, she contributes more than $400 to a family mobile phone plan shared by her immediate family and her aunt’s household.Her spending on non-essential activities remains relatively low. She spends up to $100 a week eating out with her husband, has a basic ClassPass membership, gets massages twice a month, and occasionally has manicures.Her discretionary spending usually ranges from $300 to $500 a month, although it can reach $1,000 during months when she travels.Five years after starting her content and fashion businesses, Khan has created stronger boundaries between work and personal life to avoid another period of burnout.She continues to run her businesses while living in Queens.“I don’t feel like I have to constantly burn myself out and overexert myself to prove anything to myself or others,” Khan told Business Insider.Even though New York City remains expensive, Khan has no plans to leave. She hopes to continue living in the city and raise her future family there.
Article Summary: Mohuya Khan, 27, is a content creator and business owner in Queens, New York. She generated about $130,000 in gross revenue in 2025, and kept about $70,000 after business expenses and taxes. She said managing nine sources of income while working long hours pushed her close to physical and mental exhaustion.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Dale Carnegie: "When we have accepted the worst, we have nothing more to lose. And that automatically means…" - a lesson in facing fear and uncertainty
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Dale Carnegie (Image: Wikipedia)

Quote of the day by Dale Carnegie

"When we have accepted the worst, we have nothing more to lose. And that automatically means, we have everything to gain!"

Where this quote actually comes from

What the quote by Dale Carnegie is actually saying

Why accepting the worst can genuinely shift someone's mindset

Why acceptance is genuinely not the same thing as giving up

Why fear so often makes a problem look bigger than it actually is

What "everything to gain" actually means here

How this idea applies directly to failure

Other memorable quotes by Dale Carnegie

"Inaction breeds doubt and fear. Action breeds confidence and courage."

"Our thoughts make us what we are."

"When we stop fighting the inevitable, we release energy which enables us to create a richer life."

"It isn't work that makes you tired, it's your mental attitude."

Why this quote still matters today

Fear often grows strongest exactly when someone imagines everything that could possibly go wrong. The possibility of failure can make an uncertain situation feel considerably worse than it actually is, sometimes stopping a person from taking any action at all. Dale Carnegie offered a genuinely different way of approaching a difficult situation in his book How to Stop Worrying and Start Living. "When we have accepted the worst, we have nothing more to lose," he wrote. "And that automatically means, we have everything to gain!" None of this suggests people should expect the worst or simply give up hope. Instead, Carnegie is arguing that actually accepting an unfavourable possibility can reduce the fear surrounding it considerably. Once the mind finally stops fighting the possibility of failure, there tends to be far more room left over to think clearly, make a real decision and start looking for an actual way forward.This line appears in Carnegie's own book, where he illustrates the exact idea through real stories of people who used it during genuine moments of crisis. One example he gives is Willis H. Carrier, an engineer who faced a serious professional setback and later described the effect of applying this approach directly."After facing the worst," Carrier reportedly said, "I immediately relaxed and felt a sense of peace that I hadn't experienced in days. " Carnegie also describes Earl P. Haney, who applied the same underlying principle after confronting a serious personal diagnosis, reconciling himself to the worst outcome and then deliberately trying to get the most out of whatever time remained. Carnegie summarised the whole approach as a simple three-step process, ask what the worst realistic outcome actually is, prepare yourself mentally to accept it, then calmly try to improve on the very worst you have already agreed to accept.Carnegie's message is really about reducing fear by directly confronting the exact outcome someone is most afraid of. When a person is uncertain about what might actually happen, they can spend a striking amount of time imagining increasingly negative scenarios, which tends to make the whole situation feel considerably more overwhelming than it really is. Carnegie suggests mentally acknowledging the worst realistic outcome directly. Once that outcome has genuinely been accepted, the fear surrounding it tends to lose a good deal of its power, and anything better than that outcome starts to look like a genuine gain.Imagine someone worried about losing their job. Before making any real decision, they might repeatedly picture the consequences, financial pressure, uncertainty and the difficulty of finding another position. If they instead acknowledge that losing the job is genuinely possible, and start actually considering what they would do afterward, the whole situation becomes far more concrete. They can update their CV, sharpen a skill, contact potential employers and take a proper look at their finances. The uncertainty itself has not disappeared. Their actual response to it has changed considerably.This is one of the most important distinctions running through Carnegie's message. Accepting a possible negative outcome does not mean deliberately choosing it, or stopping any effort to prevent it from happening. It means recognising honestly that the outcome is possible, rather than letting fear of it dominate every single thought. A person can accept that a business might genuinely fail while still working extremely hard to save it. Someone can acknowledge that an application may be rejected while still preparing for it carefully. Acceptance, in this sense, coexists perfectly well with genuine effort.Fear tends to operate through uncertainty. When people genuinely do not know what will happen, the mind fills in the gaps with imagined possibilities, and sometimes those imagined outcomes end up feeling far more frightening than the actual situation ever was. Confronting the worst realistic possibility places real boundaries around that uncertainty. Instead of endlessly asking what if everything goes wrong, a person can start asking what they would actually do next if it did. That single question turns fear into something closer to planning.Carnegie's second point follows naturally from the first. Once a person has already accepted the worst realistic outcome, every improvement beyond that point becomes a genuine potential gain. A failed attempt can still provide real experience. A rejection can reveal exactly what needs improving. A difficult change can open up an opportunity to try a genuinely different approach. The person may not get the exact result they originally wanted, but the situation can still contain real possibilities that were simply difficult to see while fear dominated their thinking entirely.Failure can feel genuinely devastating when someone treats it as an outcome that must never happen under any circumstances. Once failure is recognised instead as one possible part of a longer process, it becomes considerably easier to prepare for properly. None of this makes failure pleasant. It simply prevents the fear of failure from growing so powerful that it stops someone experimenting or trying at all. Many worthwhile goals involve repeated attempts, and a person who can recover from an unsuccessful one tends to learn considerably more, over time, than someone who avoids taking any risk whatsoever.Uncertainty runs through almost every major decision anyone makes. Career changes, financial choices and personal ambitions all carry some genuine possibility of failure attached to them. The instinctive response is usually to avoid thinking about the worst outcome altogether. Carnegie suggests doing very nearly the opposite, facing it directly, understanding it properly and working out exactly how you would respond if it actually happened. Once the fear of the unknown turns into a concrete possibility that can genuinely be planned for, it tends to become considerably easier to focus on whatever can still actually be achieved. The quote's real lesson was never about expecting failure. It is about reducing the power fear holds over someone by being willing to face genuine uncertainty head on.
Article Summary: Dale Carnegie's quote of the day: "When we have accepted the worst, we have nothing more to lose!" Fear often grows strongest when someone imagines everything that could possibly go wrong. Carnegie suggests mentally acknowledging the worst realistic outcome directly.

Article Title: She spent 10 months restoring a 160-year-old house; now Lauren Iraeta is reconnecting former families with pieces of their history
Article Text:
Lauren Iraeta’s home.

Restoring a sea captain’s waterfront home

Names carved inside the widow’s walk

Discovering forgotten history in the backyard

When Lauren Iraeta and her husband bought an old waterfront house, they expected to spend their weekends repairing timber and replacing outdated plumbing.Instead, after a 10-month renovation, the 44-year-old real estate agent became a historical investigator. She began researching the people who had lived in the house and reconnecting their descendants with forgotten family items and records.In an exclusive interview with PEOPLE magazine, Iraeta explained how restoring the historic home turned into a long-term effort to record the stories of the people who had lived there over the past 150 years.The couple bought the waterfront property as experienced home renovators looking for their next project. Iraeta was not immediately convinced, but the house’s unusual historic features soon changed her mind.“My husband fell in love with this house instantly and I needed a little bit of convincing,” Iraeta told PEOPLE. “The charm of the house, the front porch and the widow’s walk at the very top is something you could never find in any other house.”The physical renovation took 10 months of continuous work. The couple made structural repairs, opened some interior walls, and added two bathrooms while keeping the original character of the house.“It ended up being a huge labor of love,” Iraeta said. “The house still looks like an old house, but doesn’t have old problems.”After the renovation was finished, Iraeta began searching local records and archives. Her research suggested that the house was probably built around 1860 by a sea captain, making it much older than local town records had indicated.Her search became more interesting when she explored the widow’s walk, a rooftop feature where wives historically watched the water for ships returning home.Inside the space, earlier residents had carved and written their names into the wooden walls.“In that room on the wall are names written and carved into the wood,” Iraeta told PEOPLE. She has since created a complete list of the property’s owners and the years they lived there. “I have the name of every owner and when they lived here.”Her research eventually led her to descendants of former residents, including the elderly grandchildren of the home’s third owners. The siblings, now in their 80s and living in California, did not know that their late father had written a 10-page account of his childhood in the house and the surrounding community around 1910.Iraeta found the family and gave them a copy of the document.“Their children didn’t know this existed,” Iraeta told PEOPLE. “I recently tracked them down in California and gave them a copy.”Iraeta’s research has also helped explain physical discoveries around the property. One example is a small pet cemetery hidden in the backyard.She continues to contact descendants of former residents in an effort to learn the names and stories of the animals buried there.After 21 years as a real estate agent, Iraeta said the project has changed the way she thinks about houses and property ownership.“Knowing that every house has a story and how emotional it is when you leave a house, for whatever reason it may be, I feel fortunate to be here and feel very connected to the people that lived here before us,” Iraeta said in the PEOPLE report. “I’m excited to see what else I uncover.”
Article Summary: Lauren Iraeta and her husband bought an old waterfront house as experienced home renovators. After a 10-month renovation, the 44-year-old real estate agent became a historical investigator. She began researching the people who had lived in the house and reconnecting their descendants with forgotten family items.

Article Title: In June 2026, Washington began restoring 270 acres across two river islands; the project will reconnect the South Fork Skagit estuary to natural tides and hundreds more acres for endangered Chinook sa
Article Text:
Construction begins on project to restore estuary habitat in South Fork Skagit River (Photo by: WDFW)

Removing old dikes to restore tidal flows

Important nursery habitat for young salmon

Temporary closures and future recreation

State and federal funding

Heavy earth-moving equipment began work in June 2026 on a major coastal restoration project in Skagit County, Washington. The project will remove old sea defences and breach river levees across two islands in the South Fork Skagit River delta.The Island Unit Restoration Project, managed by the Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW), will restore 270 acres of former farmland in the Skagit Wildlife Area to natural intertidal wetlands over the next two years.By reconnecting isolated marshes to the tides, the project will remove barriers that block water movement and open access to hundreds of additional acres of intertidal estuary across the wider delta. The restored tidal channels will provide important habitat for young Puget Sound Chinook salmon, a species protected under the United States Endangered Species Act (ESA).The Island Unit is made up of two islands in the South Fork Skagit River estuary. The islands can only be reached by boat.In the early 1900s, farmers built dikes and drained the tidal wetlands to create farmland. WDFW bought the land in the 1950s and mainly managed it for wildlife, but the old structures continued to block natural water flows and fish migration routes.Engineers working on the project will remove old dikes, levees, and tidegates. This will allow saltwater from Skagit Bay and freshwater from the Skagit River’s Freshwater, Deepwater, and Steamboat sloughs to flow across the islands again.According to details released by WDFW, Aberdeen-based contractor Brumfield Construction, Inc. will also dig new internal channels, build low-angle landings for small boats, and create raised earth mounds that will stay above water during normal daily tides.Estuaries are coastal areas where freshwater rivers meet saltwater. These areas provide rich feeding grounds for fish and other wildlife.For young Chinook salmon, known as smolts, sheltered tidal channels are important places to stop and feed as they travel from rivers toward the ocean.“This project doesn’t just restore habitat on this 270-acre site; it removes barriers to reconnect hundreds more acres of intertidal estuary across the South Fork Skagit River delta,” said Jenny Baker, senior restoration specialist and project manager at WDFW, in an agency statement.“Young Chinook will quickly use these rich feeding grounds so that they grow bigger and survive better once they leave the shelter of the estuary and head out into Whidbey Basin, Puget Sound, and the ocean beyond,” Baker said.The Island Unit project follows the nearby Milltown Island Estuary Restoration Project. Earthwork on that project was completed in late 2024, while native plant restoration is still underway.Because of heavy equipment and construction activity, WDFW said the Island Unit will be closed to the public from July 2026 through autumn 2028.The nearby Skagit Headquarters Unit boat launch and parking area will also have temporary closures as construction equipment is brought to the site.Although access will be limited during construction, the final design will continue to support recreation. The area is popular with waterfowl hunters, kayakers, boaters, and wildlife photographers.“Through years of collaboration with treaty tribes, advisory group members, waterfowl hunters, and partner organizations, we’re proud of how this project balances habitat restoration for Chinook salmon recovery with continued recreational access for hunting, boating, paddling, and wildlife watching,” said Brendan Brokes, WDFW’s North Puget Sound Regional Director.After construction, the new low-angle landings will make it easier for paddlers and hunters to bring small boats ashore. The raised recreational mounds will be planted with native trees and shrubs to create more wildlife habitat.WDFW also plans to install permanent waterfowl hunting blinds on some of the mounds overlooking permanent water features.State biologists first proposed the Island Unit project in the late 2010s. Beginning in 2020, the project went through public comment periods, reviews with stakeholders, and consultations with regional treaty tribes.Construction is being paid for with a mix of state and federal funding.Federal money comes from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA), distributed through the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).State funding comes from the Puget Sound Acquisition and Restoration Fund and Washington’s Climate Commitment Act (CCA), a cap-and-invest program that supports climate resilience and pollution reduction.Earlier planning, design, and environmental permitting were funded through Washington state capital budgets, the Washington Salmon Recovery Funding Board, and the Estuary and Salmon Restoration Program (ESRP).
Article Summary: The Island Unit Restoration Project will restore 270 acres of former farmland in the Skagit Wildlife Area to natural intertidal wetlands over the next two years. The restored tidal channels will provide important habitat for young Puget Sound Chinook salmon, a species protected under the United States Endangered Species Act.

Article Title: Trump admin creates task force to crack down on birth tourism, revokes over 600 visas
Article Text:
US launches birth tourism crackdown

The US State Department has set up a new Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force to identify and act against foreign nationals suspected of travelling to the US primarily to give birth, saying it has already revoked more than 600 visas as part of the crackdown.Announcing the task force on Aug 12, the State Department said it would review the activities of visa holders worldwide, connect information held across federal agencies including the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), examine travel histories and take action against those involved in birth tourism or the networks facilitating it.The move comes amid a wider Trump administration push to prevent what it describes as the exploitation of US immigration laws through birth tourism. A few days ago on Aug 6, President Donald Trump issued two Executive Orders seeking to restrict birthright citizenship and prevent what the administration calls ‘birth tourism’. Subsequently, a coalition of civil rights groups have filed a lawsuit contending that an earlier Supreme Court ruling protecting birthright citizenship nullifies these two executive orders.The June 30 decision in the case of Trump v/s Barbara affirmed that the 14th Amendment guarantees citizenship to anyone born in the country except for the children of diplomats or enemy forces in the US.In its statement the State Department said facilitators have turned the practice of birth tourism into a for-profit industry, advertising services such as ‘birth in the US’, which includes offering an array of services such as visa coaching to conceal the purpose of travel and hospital arrangements. It also alleged that some facilitators forge medical documents or coach clients to conceal the purpose of their travel.The crackdown is, however, creating anxiety beyond those suspected of deliberately travelling to the US for childbirth. Social media groups of the Indian diaspora are filed with anxious messages.Immigrant professionals such as those on H-1B visas, spouses who hold the H-4 (dependent) visa, as well as international students who become pregnant while legally living in the US, are increasingly concerned about travelling outside the country and returning while pregnant. The concern is not that pregnancy itself violates their status, but that heightened scrutiny around birth tourism could lead to questions about their purpose of travel and ability to re-enter the US.A H-4 visa holder told TOI that she wanted to meet her parents in India, during the early stages of her pregnancy, but was worried about being questioned at the US airport on her return, and being denied re-entry in the US. Immigration attorneys view that pregnancy by itself should not result in an entry ban for such visa holders, but do not rule out additional questioning. They state that the primary focus of the crackdown will be on B visa holders, such as tourists.The State Department said the task force has uncovered cases in which travellers allegedly concealed their true purpose. In one case, a couple on two separate occasions used a conference and vacation as cover to give birth to children in the US , while in another, a foreign government official travelled ostensibly on official business but stayed three months and gave birth. Visas in both cases were revoked.The department warned that foreigners who deliberately misrepresent the purpose of their travel may become permanently ineligible for a US visa or admission.
Article Summary: US State Department has set up a new Birth Tourism Prevention Task Force to identify and act against foreign nationals suspected of travelling to the US primarily to give birth. The move comes amid a wider Trump administration push to prevent what it describes as the exploitation of US immigration laws through birth tourism.

Article Title: North America’s longest cable-stayed bridge is now open with a massive 853-metre crossing linking US and Canada
Article Text:
Gordie Howe International Bridge days before its opening, July 2026. Image Credit: Wikipedia

Why North America’s longest cable-stayed bridge is significant

The bridge in late September 2025, shown with the cranes removed from both support towers. Image Credit: Wikipedia

How was the Gordie Howe bridge designed to handle such a demanding environment

How this record-breaking border bridge is important for trade

Image Credit: Wikipedia

Is the Gordie Howe bridge only for cars and trucks

What has the project meant for nearby communities

What could the bridge mean for the future

The Gordie Howe International Bridge has opened between Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan, creating a new six-lane crossing over the Detroit River and a new link between Canada and the United States. Its 853-metre main span is the longest of any cable-stayed bridge in North America, while the full crossing stretches approximately 2.5 kilometres.The project is much larger than the bridge itself, incorporating new ports of entry on both sides of the border, approach roads and a direct highway-to-highway connection. The bridge officially opened to traffic on 27 July 2026, adding capacity to one of North America’s busiest commercial land corridors and providing another route for people, vehicles and goods moving between the two countries.The scale of the bridge is one of its most notable features. According to the Gordie Howe International Bridge project, the crossing is approximately 2.5 kilometres long and has six traffic lanes, with three lanes in each direction. Its 853-metre main span is the longest main span of any cable-stayed bridge in North America.The bridge crosses the Detroit River without piers standing in the water, with its two main towers supporting the long central span.The project also includes Canadian and US ports of entry, approach roads and the Michigan Interchange, making the bridge part of a much larger border transportation system rather than a standalone structure.The crossing is being added to an already important trade route. The Windsor-Detroit corridor is the busiest commercial land crossing between Canada and the United States, and the official project documentation says it handles almost 30% of all Canada-US trade carried by truck. The Gordie Howe International Bridge is intended to provide additional capacity and improve the movement of people and goods through the corridor.Building a long cable-stayed bridge across the Detroit River presented several engineering challenges. DYWIDAG(Dyckerhoff & Widmann AG), which supplied the stay-cable system, says the bridge was designed to cope with extreme temperature swings and the possibility of ice-galloping affecting the cables.The company describes the project as the world’s longest composite-deck stay-cable bridge, with an 853-metre main span. Because of the local climate and the scale of the structure, the cable system required specialised protection and damping measures. DYWIDAG supplied 216 stay cables for the bridge and was involved in developing the cable system alongside the wider bridge design. According to the company, the cable system and bridge geometry were developed in parallel, helping avoid redesigns and reduce design cycles.DYWIDAG also says fatigue resistance, corrosion protection and installation risks were addressed before construction, while a custom damping system was developed to meet the demands created by the local climate and structural requirements. These claims come from DYWIDAG’s own project account and describe the supplier’s role in the bridge’s engineering and construction.The bridge has been built in a region where cross-border transport is closely connected to manufacturing, particularly the automotive industry. Vehicle manufacturers and suppliers on both sides of the Canada-US border depend on the movement of parts and materials through the Windsor-Detroit corridor. The timing of these shipments can be particularly important because manufacturing operations often rely on components arriving according to tightly managed production schedules.The new bridge is intended to provide additional capacity and another major route across the Detroit River. It creates a direct highway-to-highway connection between Ontario’s Highway 401 and Michigan’s Interstate 75 through the wider Gordie Howe International Bridge project. Official project documents identify increased border-crossing capacity, improved connectivity and network redundancy among the project's transportation objectives. That additional route could also give the regional transport system greater resilience when accidents, breakdowns, congestion or other disruptions affect an existing crossing.The project also includes a dedicated multi-use path for pedestrians and cyclists. The path is separate from the vehicle lanes and is designed to connect with walking and cycling networks on both sides of the border. It is also part of the Trans Canada Trail network, giving the international crossing a recreational and active-travel function in addition to its role in commercial transportation.The pedestrian and cycling facility did not open at exactly the same time as vehicle traffic. The bridge opened to motorists on 27 July 2026, while the multi-use path opened separately later. The path allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross the Detroit River without using the vehicle lanes, although users must still complete the applicable border-processing requirements. The project has described the path as a toll-free connection intended to provide another way for people to travel between Windsor and Detroit.The project has included community investment alongside its transport role. The ‘Gordie Howe International Bridge Community Benefits Quarterly Report’ describes a $20 million Canadian-dollar Neighbourhood Infrastructure Strategy supporting communities on both sides of the border. The report says approximately $14.6 million had been allocated to 29 projects in Windsor and Detroit by 2019, while further projects were later added. Among the initiatives were improvements to local trails, tree planting, community organisation grants and support for neighbourhood programmes.The Community Benefits Plan has also supported the Delray Home Improvement Program in Detroit. By the end of the 2022-23 fiscal year, the project reported that 65 homes had either been repaired or were in the process of receiving repairs. The programme's service area was also expanded to include eligible homes in the Carbon Works neighbourhood. The C$4 million figure previously cited for the programme has been removed here because the available official source confirms the programme and its results but does not establish that precise figure clearly enough for inclusion.The opening marks the completion of a major binational infrastructure project intended to add capacity to the Windsor-Detroit transportation corridor. The bridge combines six traffic lanes, a long cable-stayed main span, new border facilities, a direct highway-to-highway connection and a multi-use path for pedestrians and cyclists.Canadian government officials have said the project is intended to strengthen supply chains, support manufacturing, improve the movement of goods and people and increase the resilience of the North American trade corridor. The longer-term importance of the bridge will depend on how it performs as part of the wider Windsor-Detroit transportation network.Its additional capacity gives commercial operators, commuters and other travellers another route across the Detroit River, while the new highway connections and border facilities are designed to make the crossing part of a more integrated transportation system. In that sense, the bridge is not only a record-setting structure. Its practical significance will ultimately be measured by how effectively it supports the movement of people and goods between Canada and the United States.
Article Summary: The Gordie Howe International Bridge has opened between Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan. Its 853-metre main span is the longest of any cable-stayed bridge in North America. The full crossing stretches approximately 2.5 kilometres and has six traffic lanes. The bridge officially opened to traffic on 27 July 2026.

Article Title: Meet Scarlett Tiani, the Connecticut student whose dog-safety invention reached US Nationals and earned a national award plus patent-application support
Article Text:
Scarlett Tiani and her amazing journey from a 5th-grade Invention Convention project at Tracey Magnet School to the national stage

Smart warnings for postal workers and neighbours

Norwalk students succeed nationally

Quinn Robertson: Inventor of The Focus Fleece, which received a national Honorable Mention.

Inventor of The Focus Fleece, which received a national Honorable Mention. Francesca Siano: Inventor of the Skier Slip N’ Clip.

Inventor of the Skier Slip N’ Clip. Eliza Z.: Inventor of The EZ Cone.

From classroom idea to patent application

A pet safety system created by a Connecticut middle school student to protect postal workers, delivery drivers, neighbours, and pets has received national recognition and legal support for a US patent application.Scarlett Tiani, a sixth-grade student at West Rocks Middle School in Norwalk, created the Tail Wag Warning to help prevent unexpected encounters between dogs and people visiting a home.Her invention won two major honours at the 2026 Invention Convention U.S. Nationals, held at the Henry Ford Museum of American Innovation in Detroit.More than 305,000 students took part in the competition nationwide, but only 513 inventors reached the national showcase. Tiani was one of just four students selected to represent Norwalk Public Schools.According to updates from Norwalk Public Schools Communications, Tiani was also one of only five inventors in the entire competition to receive the Patent Application Award, sponsored by international law firm WilmerHale. The award is worth up to $10,000 and provides free legal advice, intellectual property support, and help with submitting an official patent application for her invention.Tiani also won the Industry Innovation Award for Animal Care and Pets (K–12). She received a trophy, a personalized certificate, and a $100 cash prize.The Tail Wag Warning is a multi-level warning system designed for homes with pets.Tiani first developed the idea as a fifth-grade student in Mrs. Santaniello’s gifted and talented classroom at Tracey Magnet School.The system uses a customizable mailbox magnet with important information about a pet. It also includes a QR code that provides more details digitally. A smart warning light can show when a dog is outside, giving mail carriers, delivery drivers, first responders, and neighbours a clear warning before they enter the yard or property.According to the school district, these visual warnings and quick-access information are designed to help prevent accidental dog bites, unexpected encounters, and pets escaping from the property.Tiani travelled to Detroit as part of a four-student team from Norwalk Public Schools. The students advanced through local showcases and the Connecticut State Competition at the University of Connecticut.According to Norwalk Public Schools Communications, her fellow students also performed well:Norwalk Public Schools also reported that another group of local students has already qualified at the Connecticut Invention Convention for the next national competition.The upcoming competitors include Owen Anderson and Elliot Contessa from Rowayton Elementary School, who created X-Net. Concord Magnet School students Cole Danburg, inventor of The Flavor Mixer, and Alexandra Kraft, inventor of A Skier’s Best Bud, also qualified.Moving from a school project to a patent application supported by professional lawyers is a major achievement for a young inventor.District officials described Tiani’s journey from a Tracey Magnet School student to a national award winner as an example of what curiosity, creativity, and determination can achieve.With legal support from WilmerHale secured through her national award, Tiani will now work with intellectual property lawyers to improve her documentation and formally submit the Tail Wag Warning to the United States Patent and Trademark Office.
Article Summary: Scarlett Tiani, a sixth-grade student at West Rocks Middle School in Norwalk, created the Tail Wag Warning to help prevent unexpected encounters between dogs and people visiting a home. Her invention won two major honours at the 2026 Invention Convention U.S. Nationals, held at the Henry Ford Museum of American Innovation in Detroit. Tiani was also one of only five inventors in the entire competition to receive the Patent Application Award.

Article Title: In 1964, Elizabeth Hird and her husband bought Connecticut's Outer Island; in 1995 she donated it in his memory so it could remain protected for wildlife, research and education
Article Text:
Connecticut's Outer Island (Image Credit: outerisland.org)

From summer retreat to protected island

Hird’s conservation vision

Elizabeth Hird and her husband Basil Rauch (Image Credit: outerisland.org)

A living classroom

A legacy that continues

In 1964, Elizabeth Hird and her husband, Basil Rauch, purchased Outer Island as a summer retreat in Connecticut's Thimble Islands. More than three decades later, Hird made a decision that transformed the island's future: in 1995, she donated it to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in memory of her late husband. According to the Outer Island website's history, her goal was to protect the island's natural resources while ensuring it could continue to support education and research.Outer Island lies off the coast of Branford, Connecticut, and is the southernmost of the Thimble Islands. The five-acre island is characterised by granite outcroppings, boulder and cobble beaches, intertidal areas and small salt marshes. Today, it forms part of the Stewart B. McKinney National Wildlife Refuge.The island's history stretches back much further than Hird's ownership. According to the Outer Island history, glaciers helped shape its landscape thousands of years ago, leaving exposed granite bedrock and large boulders behind. The Mattabesic Native Americans who lived in the Stony Creek area also used the Thimble Islands during the summer and called Outer Island "Two Tree Island," referring to two prominent pine trees that once stood there.In 1889, Addison Verrill, Yale's first professor of zoology, purchased the island and spent summers there with his family. A later fire destroyed the house, but its large stone fireplace and chimney survived and were incorporated into the present building.Elizabeth Hird and Basil Rauch became the island's owners in 1964. Rauch was a professor of history at Columbia University, while Hird was an architect, artist and active conservationist. According to The Outer Island history, the couple used the property as a summer retreat before Hird ultimately decided that its future should extend beyond private ownership.In 1995, after Rauch's death, Hird donated Outer Island to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service confirms that the island had been privately owned until 1995, when Hird donated it to the refuge to protect its natural resources and provide access for education and research.The donation was more than a transfer of property. It reflected Hird's desire to preserve a place where people could study the natural environment and learn directly from it. The Outer Island history notes that she continued to use the island as her summer home until her death in 2002, at age 87.Hird's vision continues through educational and research programs conducted on the island. According to The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Outer Island provides habitat for migratory birds, marine life and serves as an important pollinator stopover site. Its varied landscape also makes it useful for exploring coastal and intertidal ecosystems.The island's education facilities include a laboratory where students can examine organisms and test water quality. A pavilion also provides an outdoor space for visitors and student groups. According to the Outer Island history, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service works with the Connecticut State University System and Friends of Outer Island on research and education programs.That partnership gives students opportunities to experience the Long Island Sound environment directly rather than studying it only in classrooms. Guided visits can help educators connect lessons about ecology, geology and marine life with the landscape around them.Hird's donation changed Outer Island from a privately owned summer retreat into a protected place with a broader public purpose. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service lists the 1995 donation as an important milestone in the history of the Stewart B. McKinney National Wildlife Refuge, noting that Hird wanted the island to be used for education and Long Island Sound research.Today, Outer Island remains both a wildlife habitat and an outdoor learning environment. Its protected shoreline, intertidal areas and small salt marshes provide space for wildlife, while its educational facilities allow students, researchers and visitors to explore the natural systems that surround the island.What began in 1964 as a couple's summer retreat ultimately became a lasting conservation legacy. By donating Outer Island to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in memory of her husband, Elizabeth Hird ensured that the island would remain protected while continuing to teach future generations about Connecticut's coastal environment.
Article Summary: Outer Island lies off the coast of Branford, Connecticut, and is the southernmost of the Thimble Islands. The five-acre island is characterised by granite outcroppings, boulder and cobble beaches, intertidal areas and small salt marshes. In 1995, Elizabeth Hird donated Outer Island to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in memory of her late husband, Basil Rauch.

Article Title: A 112-acre New Jersey restoration project is planting about 50,000 native trees and shrubs, creating vernal pools and rebuilding Raritan River floodplain habitat
Article Text:
Trees laid out at the site for planting (FWS photos)

Settlement led to restoration

Transforming the 112-acre site

A map of the proposed restoration area

Helping wildlife

Contamination behind restoration

A 112-acre restoration project has begun along the Raritan River in New Jersey, with the aim of bringing back forest and wetland habitat that was affected by contamination linked to the American Cyanamid Superfund Site. The project is being carried out under a settlement related to damage to natural resources.According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), the project is taking place on land owned by Duke Farms, a centre of the Doris Duke Foundation, in Hillsborough, New Jersey. The site is about 2.8 miles upstream from the American Cyanamid Site. The work will convert retired agricultural fields into forested and scrub-shrub floodplain habitat next to the Raritan River.The restoration is part of a larger effort to compensate for natural resources that were lost or injured because of contamination from the American Cyanamid Site. The work will include planting native trees and shrubs, controlling invasive plants and creating habitat for amphibians, insects, birds and other wildlife.The project follows a settlement finalised on July 16, 2024, between the US Department of Justice, the State of New Jersey and Wyeth Holdings LLC.The settlement addresses liability for past releases of hazardous substances at or near the American Cyanamid Superfund Site in Bridgewater, New Jersey.The releases affected several types of habitat near the Raritan River, including floodplain, riparian, upland and wetland areas.The US Fish and Wildlife Service, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the NJDEP are the Natural Resource Trustees for the American Cyanamid Site. The Trustees will use the settlement to support the restoration project and its monitoring.A major part of the project will be the planting of about 50,000 native trees and shrubs. The former agricultural fields will gradually be converted into floodplain forest and scrub-shrub habitat.The project will also involve intensive management of undesirable invasive plants. These plants can interfere with the growth of native vegetation, so controlling them will be an important part of establishing the restored habitat.A deer fence will be installed around the project area to protect newly planted vegetation from herbivory, or damage caused when animals feed on plants.The project will also create three acres of vernal pool habitat. Vernal pools are temporary pools of water that can provide habitat for amphibians. Native grass and pollinator seed mixes will also be planted to provide food sources for insects and other pollinators.The restoration will not end when the planting and construction work is completed. The project includes 15 years of monitoring and adaptive management. This means the site will continue to be watched and managed so that the restoration work can be assessed and adjusted when needed.Floodplain forests are among the most biologically diverse habitats in the region. However, they have also been historically degraded. The restoration is expected to help re-establish floodplain forest in the area. This will provide improved habitat for wildlife, including birds, bats and amphibians.The Service is also carrying out effectiveness monitoring with Duke Farms. The monitoring will look at the benefits that improved habitat provides to bird species and other wetland resources. The information gathered through this work can also help guide future restoration projects.The project is expected to provide benefits beyond wildlife habitat. The restoration could also improve the water quality of the Raritan River and increase flood storage capacity and storm resiliency. It is also expected to improve ecosystem services that benefit local communities.The restoration project is connected to contamination caused by industrial activity at the American Cyanamid Site. Releases from the site contaminated soil and groundwater with several hazardous substances.These included volatile organic compounds, semi-volatile organic compounds, polychlorinated biphenyls, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, cyanide and heavy metals.The releases also affected the Raritan River and Cuckels Brook, a tributary of the Raritan River. Associated sediments, groundwater, wetlands, riparian areas, floodplains and uplands were also affected.The contamination resulted in potential injury to fish and wildlife. The restoration work is therefore intended to compensate for losses and injuries to natural resources in floodplain, riparian and wetland habitats.The floodplain reforestation project is not the first restoration work connected to the American Cyanamid Site. The Trustees had earlier identified two projects to compensate for injury to the river caused by the facility. One involved removing the Weston Mill Dam on the Millstone River. The other involved a design and feasibility study looking at ways to improve fish passage at the Island Farm Weir. The weir was identified as the remaining barrier to migratory fish passage in the lower 30 miles of the Raritan River.The Trustees and the potentially responsible party reached a settlement in 2017. That settlement included the implementation of the two projects and provided a limited release for in-river injury caused by the discharge of hazardous substances from the American Cyanamid Site. Both of those restoration objectives have now been completed.
Article Summary: A 112-acre restoration project has begun along the Raritan River in New Jersey. It aims to bring back forest and wetland habitat that was affected by contamination linked to the American Cyanamid Superfund Site. The project is being carried out under a settlement related to damage to natural resources. The work will include planting native trees and shrubs, controlling invasive plants and creating habitat for amphibians, insects and birds.

Article Title: Michigan's historic Ford House is replacing concrete shoreline with natural habitat; the $7 million project will restore 1 mile of shore and 17.5 acres of aquatic and wetland habitat
Article Text:
Excavator installing a fish lunker on Ford Cove. Credit: Ford House

Removing concrete barriers to bring back native species

Shoreline hardening at Ford House prior to construction. Credit: NOAA Fisheries/Terry Heatlie

Rebuilding a layered ecosystem
